utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, would you have the accused brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody hear me? Does the Office of the Prosecutor hear? Do the defence hear? Mr. Blaskic, do you hear? GENERAL BLASKIC: Yes, your Honour, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Perhaps the Office of the Prosecutor is now -- today is it made up of the same people? Has anybody changed? Are you the same? Yes, all right. The Defence, there is the same composition of attorneys. So I think everything is now ready for us to begin. Mr. Prosecutor, our schedule was a bit upset, as you remember, because the first witness could not stay here and we decided that we would postpone the cross-examination. Mr. Simon Leach also was interrupted. Where are we now? What is today's schedule for today? I want to say this both for the Prosecutor and the Defence. There will be a certain number of interruptions that are out of our control, unfortunately, so long as we have only one court room. That is on Thursday almost the entire day and Friday afternoon apparently we are not going to be able to meet. So turning to the Prosecutor, how are we going to organise our work?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel, good morning. We are going to commence this morning with the cross-examination of Mr. Donia, and when that is complete we will then continue with Mr. Leach. We do have other witnesses for the rest of the week and we will fit in with the schedule as best we can but we do have witnesses to fill this week. As a preliminary matter, Mr. President, the abridged translations that you received in French have now been completed, so I would like to submit those in evidence. They are part of Exhibit 38B. I think there were five in all. I have those in complete form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Does the Defence have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This, you will remember, Mr. President, is relevant to the testimony of Dr. Zoran Pajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Thank you. Registrar, have you put in the documents? I think that one of them was actually published. (Handed) Thank you. All right. Then I will put it in my binder. All right. Perhaps we can begin, start by having the witness brought in. We are now talking about Mr. Robert Donia, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. President. I will now hand over to my co-counsel, Mr. Kehoe. (Witness enters court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, first of all, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Kehoe, do you want to begin the questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, our last session with Mr. Donia, I believe it was on 25th June, we completed our examination of Mr. Donia and he was being tendered for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's what I had thought, but since we had not met, I wasn't sure whether you wanted to add something. I thought you had completed that. All right. Now the floor is now Mr. Nobilo's or Mr. Hayman, but I see Mr. Nobilo getting up, so I can give you the floor to have the witness answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Donia, we shall go back to the beginning of your testimony, so as to facilitate the task of my colleagues and their Honours. On page 65 of the transcript -- I shall not quote it, but I should like to refer to it in brief -- you said that from 1972 until 1976 and later from 1974 to 1975 you had done some research in the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I would like to know regarding this period from 1974-1975 which archives exactly you went to and precisely which segment of history you studied and what exactly you were doing in the archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was awarded a Fullbright Research Scholarship in 1974 for the academic year of 1974-1975. My principal topic during that time was the Muslim Movement for Cultural and Religous Autonomy, which took place from 1899-1910. My research was principally in the Arki Bosni Herzegovina, in the collections of documents that were generated by the Austro-Hungarian authorities at that time in early 20th century. I also at that time worked in the National Library, National and University Library in Sarajevo. I also worked with considerable less time in archives in Belgrade, Zagreb, Budapest, Vienna, London and Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder which languages can you use in addition to English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of that research was in the German language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. That question was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe? You wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That question was not translated. I didn't hear the translation. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There was an interpretation problem for a moment. Let me turn to the booth. Mr. Nobilo, will you ask your question again please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. The question was: which language in addition to his native English can he use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: German and the language formerly known as Serbo-Croatian, now known either as Bosnian, Serbian or Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Further on, on page 67 of the transcript, you spoke about your research from November 1994, when you made several trips to Bosnia and one to Croatia and when you had a series of contacts with your colleagues, making interviews and continuing your research. I am interested again in learning which institutions and which individuals you contacted and whom you interviewed, if you could be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a rather long list, but in terms of the institutions that I contacted and worked with, they were principally the Institute for History in Sarajevo, the Filosofski Fakultat or Philosophy Faculty at the University of Sarajevo and Academy of Sciences of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As for the interviews, did you interview persons who were participants in the events from 1990 to 1994/1995, or when you mention interviews, are you referring to interviews with your colleagues, scholars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both. I have interviewed some participants in political events from 1990 on. I have interviewed Mayor Beslagic of Tuzla. I interviewed Mr. Stjepan Kljuic and several political leaders in both the Tuzla and Mostar areas for articles that I subsequently published in Transition Magazine. I have also begun and not completed a project to interview former mayors of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you mention Mostar, can you recall whom you talked to in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke with the rector and pro-rector of the university of Mostar in west Mostar. The rector's name was Professor Kordic. I can't recall the pro-rector's name at this time, although it is in my article. I spoke briefly with the Director of the newly opened national library in west Mostar and the rector of the University of Mostar in the east, Mr. Slipcavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. The company that you are working in, does it have any business relationships with the Government of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None. None.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief you claimed that the South Slavs tribes came to the Balkans and that today's territory of Croatia and Bosnia were inhabited by south Slavs. I would like to know whether those tribes bore any names? Do we know the names of those tribes so that we might identify them, the tribes, the South Slavs tribes that settled there and began to live in the territory of today's Bosnia and today's Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think many of us would like to know all those names and I would just preface my answer by saying that sources are very scarce and to some degree unreliable. Probably the most important document which identifies names of tribes is the manuscript of Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, who died in 959. In his document he reports at least two names, those of the Croats and Serbs as tribes that migrated from the areas that I indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Furthermore, you mentioned Cyrillus and Methodias, who were Orthodox missionaries. Can you remind us of the dates of their lives and work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mission was normally dated as 863. I do not know the dates of the lives, birth and death of either one of them. I'm not certain that they are known with great certainty by any scholars, but I do not have them at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because how can you defend your claim that they are Orthodox missionaries when the split into Catholicism and Orthodoxy occurred in 1054?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you raise a good point and at that time the church was certainly divided into two parts, but not formally completely split. They were missionaries who were sent out from Constantinople and therefore associated with that Eastern Orthodox cultural and religious orientation but your point that the church was not yet at that point divided is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about Hungarian authority gaining control of Bosnia, so I would like to hear your assessment of the Pacta Conventa of 1104, whether you are familiar with that document and how you view it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1102 is the normal date that's attributed to the Pacta Conventa, and it is a document that brings the Croatian nobility into an agreement with the Crown of Hungary. Its character has been critiqued by Nada Klaic, Professor Nada Klaic, a Croatian historian, who died in the late 1980s, who points out that the date of that document, our actual document that we have, is from a considerably later time, and therefore may have some characteristics in it that are more properly characteristic of the, say, late 13th century than the 12th. However, the document in so far as it speaks to developments in the 12th century or 1102 states that the nobility or noble families of Croatia agreed to accept the authority of the Hungarian Crown and thereafter the Crown of Hungary became known as -- the King of Hungary became known as the King of Hungary and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you define the Hungarian Crown of Saint Stephen as a personal union or something else; in other words, was the Hungarian king, king of Hungary and Croatia or of a subordinate Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. The title of Ban, you said that it was used as an indication of something like a governor among the South Slavs. Could you please try and be more precise and say among which tribes and in which regions was this title of "Ban" used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A second question: did the Serbs and Bulgarians have the same title of Ban? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know who was the first well-known Ban of Bosnia, who has gone down in history?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I indicated in my testimony, Kulin Ban is normally the person indicated as the most important of those Bans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But not the first? Are you familiar with Ban Boric from 1154 as the first Ban in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with that name. I do not know that this is something that is known with certainty, that he was the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the founder of the Kotromanic dynasty, Ban Prijezda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we pass on to the Bogomils, please? Can you explain where this expression comes from, the expression of Bogomils, and why do you describe the Bosnian church with the term Bogomils?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have specifically not described the Bosnian church with the term Bogomil. In fact, I said that scholars disagree on this point and my own inclination is to discount reports and sources which suggest that the Bosnian church is Bogomil.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you define it, for you said that the Bosnian church was between the Catholic church and the Orthodox church that was established in between? In what sense do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a church that was created to be independent of role, and yet it never really became a court church in the Bosnian State. It is variously described by scholars as a church which had very simple practices, some of which corresponded to conventional Catholicism, and some of which may not have, but others talk about it as a largely monastic type of church organisation. It probably never had a great reach or powerful impact on the population, according to the rather fragmentary sources that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But could you please explain, because you said that it was between Catholicism and Orthodoxy, in what sense? What did it have from Orthodoxy and what was its relationship towards Orthodoxy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour, if counsel is referring to a portion in the transcript, I think it is probably more accurate to give the page and the line so the witness, if need be, and certainly the Prosecutor can reference that particular section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but for the time being the witness has not complained about anything. I think that he was able to answer. He was able to see what was what and he'll know when he has to say that he wants this or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, your Honour. It was more for my reference point in the transcript to follow exactly where defence counsel is questioning in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So really it is an objection for yourself then. Mr. Nobilo perhaps could provide us with some more details, if he thinks it would be appropriate, in order to facilitate the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is page 85 of the transcript lines 1-7 -- or 5-7, which refers exactly to the Bosnian church, and its relationships with Catholicism and Orthodoxy. That is why I am trying to obtain some clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: To interrupt you just for a moment, I have to confer with my colleagues. (Pause.) All right. Go on, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, my question had to do with the relationship with Orthodoxy. Is there anything specific in that relationship? What did it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe -- I'm sorry I do not have a copy of the transcript in front of me. Perhaps it would be helpful. I believe you're referring to a statement that I made that the Bosnian church was on the fault line between the Catholic and Orthodox worlds, between the western and eastern worlds; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. What is the context of the position of the Bosnian church on that fault line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made that statement to indicate that the church was in neither sphere in the firm sense of the word. It had practices which appeared to be very undeveloped. It had -- first of all, the sources that we have on this are exclusively, almost exclusively foreign sources, which had a vested interest in portraying that Bosnian church as heretical, that is as believing in a dualist heresy that was then widespread in Bulgaria. This has been seized upon, if you will; it has been adopted by many in the present century as evidence of a separate ecclesiastical organisation that preceded conversions to Islam. The evidence regarding the Bosnian church, as I indicated, is heavily contested. I certainly did not mean to imply that it somehow mixed and matched Orthodox and Catholic practices in some way, because we do not know much about the practices of the Bosnian church, and I referred to that only in the sense that in the general sense that to the east Orthodoxy tended to flourish and to the west of the Bosnian church, and I would say to the south to some degree Catholicism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have understood that. Thank you. You mentioned heresy. Do you accept that the Bosnian church had the characteristic of dual heresy, or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not accept the notion that it was dualist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge can you ascertain what per cent of the population belonged to the Bosnian church at the time when the Turks arrived in the Balkans? Let's just put it: was it a minority or a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not -- that's a difficult question to address in percentage terms, but at the time that the Ottomans can be said to conquer Bosnia, the Bosnian church was a dying institution. It had allegiance in only a few areas of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. In several places, like on page 110 of the transcript, you mentioned the Bosnia theory of the origins of the Bosnia in the Bogomil movement. Can you comment on this theory? Do you consider it well-founded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are many different versions of that theory. I would limit, I guess, my comment to say that the existence of a widespread dualist heresy in Bosnia prior to the Ottoman invasion does not have the unanimous support of scholars, and therefore it's not a universally accepted viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On page 113 of the transcript you mention the Orthodox Serbs who migrated to Bosnia and then later to Croatia in the part known later as Krajina, and since you do not give the names of these tribes, why do you refer to these Orthodox migrants as Serbs? Are there any other names for these new immigrants there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I note one assumption in your question that I could not give the names of the tribes. I believe I just did give you some names. The people who migrated, let us say, the ethnicity or nature and identity of them is again debated. The scholarship divides between those who would characterise them as Serbs and those who would characterise them as Vlaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On page 124 of the transcript you started talking about the modern concept of the nation, that is the establishment of the nation. You said the first phase was a cultural community based for the most part on common language. With respect to that my question is: do you know what language was spoken in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in these territories of ours? The population there, do you know what language they spoke, and then do you know anything about the speeches and the dialects, and here I am referring to the Jaikaviza (sic) and Aikaviza (sic) and also the Cakisto (sic) based dialect and is there anything to be gleaned with respect to the population breakdown based on these language differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear these questions there. The first one was: what is the name of the language that was spoken in Bosnia? I would have to say that without a time-frame it's very difficult to even give a speculative answer to that question. The second question pertained to dialects, and the particular Stokavski and Kajkavski dialects. I will tell you I am not a linguist and would only give you a speculative answer in that area. Your third question was: is anything to be gleaned from that information? I would say that some scholars have gleaned a great deal from it. I'm not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Maybe I can assist you with respect to the language spoken there during the Ottoman Empire?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question and I ask counsel just to ask questions as opposed to commentary or speeches preliminary to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: With your permission, the expert witness Donia said he could not speak to the language issue unless we specified the period. Therefore, I asked the question specifying the time period of the Ottoman Empire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think the best answer to that question is that the most common language in Bosnia during the Ottoman period was Slavic, and various people will attempt to assign a more specific word to that Slavic language. I would also note that other languages were spoken. Turkish was certainly spoken by the administrative elite, particularly as the Ottoman Empire administration took hold, and there was some Spanish in the Sephardic Jewish communities, but the primary language spoken by most people I would characterise as Slavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm interested when the Bosniaks or Muslims, depending on how you use the term, did articulate their idea of a statehood, in other words when did this nation start to be established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are two different questions. The first is when did they articulate their notion of a statehood and I would say that there are signs of a Bosnian Muslim separatist state in the early 19th century. The actual Bosnian Muslim nationalist movement, as I think of it, really comes about in the 1960s, very, very late relative to the other national movements. The question of when the Bosnian Muslims began to develop as a separate entity I think is an entirely different one and probably goes back to some time prior to the 19th century during Ottoman Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You stated that the idea of statehood first appeared in the 19th century. Can you specify a name or a group that advanced such a demand or claim, something more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On page 127 of the transcript you spoke of the delegates in the Yugoslav assembly of 1920, and you said that the majority of the Bosniaks did identify themselves as Croats. Do you know exactly how many delegates were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact number. The number of delegates was around 40 and the number of Muslim delegates who declared themselves as Croats was, I think, in the low 20s, just barely a majority. I emphasised in making that point that the notion of identifying with a nationality on the part of the Bosnian Muslim political elite was a very limited phenomenon, and confined to intellectuals and participants in political processes and was not reflective of the broader population. I also emphasised that those identities were frequently subject to change, because there were rather superficial and fleeting. The actual numbers are provided in Atif Pulvatra's book, which is called "The Yugoslav Muslim Organisation" and he does give those exact numbers. I just do not have them at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said 40 delegates. Were there 40 delegates in the Parliament or just the 40 Muslims? I did not understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said about 40, and this would be the number of Bosnian Muslim delegates in the constituent assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you: we come to the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. You did not specify very much the inter-ethnic relationships in Yugoslavia of that period. Can you describe them in some detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's again a very challenging question. The kingdom was established with the Karadordevic dynasty at its head and much of the military and administrative apparatus was under the control of Serbs. There was certainly throughout the kingdom's history a Serbian domination of the administrative and military corps that set the tone for much of what took place. The Croatian portion of the empire, while I think the Croats can be said to have entered the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes with some enthusiasm, many of them came to feel that this was not the best deal in terms of what their expectations had been for a South Slavs kingdom. The Slovenes to some degree felt the same. I would emphasise in all of this there are variations over time in how these peoples felt and it's very difficult to characterise ethnic relations at any given time with this kind of generalisation. The Bosnian Muslim political leadership generally found itself in support of the kingdom and the coalition that was in power. It was frequently a member of the ruling coalition, and the leader of the Bosnian Muslims, Mehmed Spaho, until his death in 1939, was represented in a number of the cabinets of the Yugoslav kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is obvious that we are talking about an extended period of time, but was at any point in the history of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia national equality really established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know was there violence which was related to the inter-ethnic relations in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I mentioned in my direct testimony the killing of Stjepan Radic in Parliament in -- the assassination of him in Parliament. He died, of course, some time later, but that was certainly a factor. You know, there were numerous demonstrations at various times in the history of the kingdom in all of the capital cities, in the capital cities of the primary areas, including Zagreb and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And other forms of oppression that ended in death, the conflict with the armed forces of the kingdom and the non-Serb parts of the population, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to move to the dictatorship of 6th January 1929. Why did the kingdom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The name -- what number -- the answer is a bit ambiguous here. You asked whether there was oppression committed by the royal army. Do you hear what I'm saying, Mr. Nobilo? You asked the witness whether there had been any oppression carried out by the royal army but then you added "can you answer?". Then he said "no". I myself do not know whether the answer "no" given by the witness was no, there was no repression or no, I do not know. I do not know how to answer that question. Mr. Donia, what did that "no" refer to? It was "no, I do not know" or "no, there was no repression"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is no, I do not know what the question is referring to. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So we are moving on to page 134 of the transcript, the introduction of the royal dictatorship on 6th January 1929. Can you give us some reasons for this dictatorship being introduced at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Royal House concluded that the open system of Parliamentary confrontation between representatives of the various parties was basically a downhill spiral, and was leading nowhere. Thus the dictatorship was an effort to defuse national conflicts and remove national aspirations from the political agenda. The dictatorship was accompanied by a ban on the Communist Party and a ban on parties with an ethnic or national or religious identity. Consequently most existing political formations in the kingdom of the Croats -- of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes were at that point outlawed. So clearly the hope of the monarchy was to remove nationality as a source of agitation and instability in the realm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, this dictatorship was aiming to rescue Yugoslavia; is that a correct inference that I am making, that is to prevent its break-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think also and preserve the position of the Royal Family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Referring to the assassination of Radic in the assembly, the Croat political leader, do you know the circumstances? Who assassinated him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was assassinated by a Montenegrin, who is usually described in these books as a crazed person, a Montenegrin clearly motivated in some fashion by a feeling of allegiance to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know his subsequent fate? Was he tried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Further on page 134 of the transcript you said that Radic was a controversial figure. Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a very charismatic figure. He was a very emotional speaker, aroused great passion both in his supporters and those who were critical of him. He became very controversial by his travels abroad and his flirtations with the Russians or the Soviets and his general tendency to spend a certain amount of time out of the country or in contact with foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know what were the electoral results that he had? Do you know the last elections in which -- what were the results that he got?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you specifics. I would note that the Croatian Peasant Party, of which he was the head until his death, experienced great success in the areas with Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We're moving to the Banovina, the often mentioned Banovina Croatia. Can you tell me what reasons do you see for the creation of the Banovina in the context of the sequence of events in the Yugoslav kingdom? What was what was the reason for the establishment of the Banovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there are several reasons that the negotiations were initiated and the Banovina plan subsequently adopted. One was certainly the international situation in which the pressure on Yugoslavia from Germany was being intense and the desire of the monarchy and circles in support of the monarchy was strong to reach an understanding with the Croatian leadership which would allow Yugoslavia to survive and remain independent and avoid any kind of further German meddling or possibly even a German invasion. That probably was the most pressing issue to be addressed at that time, and again there were numerous other reasons. The need of the monarchy to find a viable, on-going political compromise internally was important and to generally defuse the growing political controversies domestically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You gave us two reasons that the King, that is the Royal House, may have had for accepting the Banovina. Why did the Croats demand the Banovina? What were their reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again I think there were several. They hoped to achieve a status equal to the Serbs in the Royal Kingdom and achieve a greater territorial autonomy, if you will, over areas that they perceived to be inhabited by Croats. The actual negotiations reveal a very, I think, determined and consistent strategy, if you will, by Vladko Majic, the Croatian Peasant Party leader who had succeeded Radic, to achieve as much territorial gain for the Croatian Banovina as possible. There were some discussions of plebiscites to determine exactly what areas would go into which entity. Those were never held, as the pressure of reaching an agreement intensified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We're moving on to page 140 of the transcript. You stated there that many Croats, including Franjo Tudjman, the President, never in their heart accepted the borders of 1945. Can you tell me when did Croatia recognise Bosnia and did it recognise Bosnia within its borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd just like to note that your question presumes that I -- that was my statement. I believe that my statement was a quote from Lord David Owen, who observed that Tudjman in his heart had never accepted that as expressed in his recent book, "Balkan odyssey". There was a second question there, which was when Croatia recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina and the answer is April 7th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My apologies. Indeed this is a quote from Lord Owen. I did not mean to put it in your mouth. Can you tell me when was Bosnia founded as a State; in other words, when did it proclaim its independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: April 6th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is Montenegro and Serbia, have they recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina within its borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'm not sure of the date. They have, but I can't give you the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view was the Croatian national question better resolved in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia with the Banovina or in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia after 1945?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that I can make that assessment. In the long run I do not think it was satisfactorily solved in either political configuration, certainly not to everyone's satisfaction. Again one would have to look at in discussing the socialist period exactly the time-frame, because there certainly were times when nationality relations were better than others in the course of the socialist era.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But generally speaking could you make an assessment, up to the elections of 1990, if you can?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't make that assessment. It's difficult to make that judgement, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke of imagine I have, who succeeded Radic and his contacts with Mussolini's Italy. Do you know what happened to Majic, what was his personal fate after the Italians and Germans conquered the Kingdom of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He actually played a role in the coup of March 27th, 1941, briefly supported the new regime, which was Ante-German and committed to resisting Nazi attack. At that time when the Germans invaded he was absolutely sent to his village for a period of time. He then ended up in the camp at Jasenovac for a period of time but did not perish there. He subsequently left and I believe went to Canada, where he died in 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You went on to say that Hitler and Germany were not satisfied with Yugoslavia on April 6th and attacked Yugoslavia. Could you explain what happened, which were the events which preceded the attack, the German attack against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On March 27th a coup took place directed or under the leadership of two Yugoslav air force generals, one of whom was general Dusan Simovic. That coup to some degree took place under popular pressure and resulted in Prince Paul, the regent, fleeing the country and the 17 year old King Peter coming to power for a very few days. This was in part due to the unhappiness of the public broadly in the Yugoslav kingdom with Yugoslavia's adherence to the tripartite packet. The coup took place and large demonstrations in Belgrade indicated very popular support for resistance to Germany. This was a flash point for Hitler, who subsequently organised and directed the invasion of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you aware who was behind the organisation of the demonstrations in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Communist Party played a major role.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the British intelligence service, have you any information that they participated in any way in organising those demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They certainly did, and had various people who were being paid in various ways. I think it's probably an exaggeration to call this a British engineered coup, because there was great popular support for it, but at the same time there was an instrumental important role played by England in this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. In this connection the Communist Party, when and prompted by which event did it proclaim the resistance against the Germans after this invasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's again some debate about that, but the actual declaration of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia awaited the German invasion of the Soviet Union, which took place, I think, on June 21st, if I'm not mistaken, 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That's right, yes, yes. My next question: when the Germans attacked Yugoslavia, was there any serious armed resistance against the Germans and the Italians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was and, of course, as we know, it lasted throughout the war. That resistance was in the first instance organised by Colonel Mohilovic and the movement known as the Chetniks, which was loyal to the Royal Family, and which had the endorsement of the government in exile in London. At the same time the partisan movement under Tito gained momentum and subsequently came to pose a much more serious challenge to the allied forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I apologise. Maybe my question wasn't clear enough. I was trying to get an answer to the question of did the Royal Yugoslav Army put up any serious resistance when the actual attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you analyse why the State surrendered without any battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think there were many reasons, and I cannot subscribe to a stab in the back theory by any nationality or group for that. The fact is that the Royal Army did not put up much resistance, but that resistance, which was a very popular one, of course, picked up shortly thereafter, and subsequently had a very major impact on events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you agree with the view that the army simply broke up or did it withdraw in an organised fashion and then later organise resistance? I'm talking about the Royal Army as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's somewhere in between. Your point that there was no organised resistance initially by the Royal Army I think is a valid one, and it rather quickly dispersed. It was not, you know, a glorious moment in the history of the Yugoslav Royal Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know what was the main reason why this army dispersed, why it didn't put up any resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I've said, I think there are a number of reasons. It was certainly not prepared to confront the dimensions of this challenge, as was the case in other places in Eastern Europe as well, and was not organised in any way for a kind of a resistance movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned on page 43 that the Ustashas in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia were becoming an increasingly important factor or something to that effect. Could you perhaps be more specific in assessing the strength of the Ustashas within the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, that is until the invasion of the Germans, how numerous they were, how strong their organisation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without the transcript in front of me I do not know my specific words, but I think I indicated that they were a destabilising force. The fact is that they were --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Exactly. That's right. It was a destabilising force in Yugoslavia and the sentence before that says: "The growing presence of the Ustashas became a factor"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the Ustasha, after the assassination of 1934, at which time the Ustasha had real strong Italian sponsorship, after that assassination of Alexander, the Ustashas were principally confined to an island off Italy and as, let us say, a terrorist or potential military force really played no significant role. They were certainly there as a potential threat to the monarchy and the stability of the regime, but I think in saying that they were a growing presence I probably misstated their numerical strength within Yugoslavia as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know how many Ustashas there were in 1941, for instance, in Italy, when they came to Croatia? How many of them came from Italy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know that number. It's in the hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. After the Ustashas came into power, on page 145, you speak of the support and popularity of the Ustashas. What does that mean for you? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially in the very early days of the creation of the independent state of Croatia I think there was a general feeling amongst the Croatian population that this was for the first time an independent Croatian state. Now there were no public opinion polls taken that I know of in these early days, and none, in fact, during the whole period that would tell us how widespread this belief was but a number of observers, based on commentary in the press and elsewhere, have noted that this was a brief moment where there was some enthusiasm or support for the notion of an independent Croatian state. It didn't last very long. In the first place the role agreement, which was in May of 1941, seriously discredited the Ustasha regime, because in that agreement a large portion of the Dalmatian coast was given over to Italy and, of course, Dalmatia was the historic home of the Croatian kingdom and therefore this appeared to the wider population to be an indication of the dependence of the Ustasha on the axis powers. Furthermore, their methods soon led them to a position of unpopularity with a great deal of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of course there were no popular opinion polls, but is it possible to make any conclusions regarding the popularity and strength of the Ustasha movement as compared to the partisan movement, based on the strength and the units of the partisan movement in Croatia if we look at 1942, 1943, 1944 and 1945? Can you make any conclusions on that basis on the popularity of the Ustasha as opposed to the partisans among the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the partisans won, and they did so by, as I have indicated, several policies which insisted on the equality of nations and the policy of utmost resistance to the occupying powers. There is clearly a trend from 1941 until 1945, perhaps not in a single straight line, but nevertheless a decline in Ustasha strength and a rise in the popularity and effectiveness of the partisans in Croatia and in Bosnia in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. If we analyse the partisan movement in Croatia and Bosnia in relation to the strength of the partisan movement in other parts of Yugoslavia, is it possible to make any conclusions and any comparisons there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly the partisan movement was strong in both Bosnia and Croatia. Much of the combat that took place between the partisans and the German occupiers in particular took place in Bosnia and the participation of all nationalities in Bosnia and of Croats in the partisan movement was very strong, possibly in numerical terms stronger in some other parts of Yugoslavia, but it should be emphasised that this was a movement that had widespread participation and strong support from all nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe due to my lack of knowledge of the English language I didn't clearly understand what you said in connection with Ustasha brutalities and a reference to the current President of Croatia, President Tudjman. What movement did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a partisan in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, speaking about Dr. Franjo Tudjman, you said that he gave a lower number of victims of the independent Croatia which was lower than was currently believed and currently used. Which is more realistic? Could you comment on that, his assessment or the current one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There have been numerous attempts to arrive at a fairly precise number of war dead and those who were victims both of the camp at Jasenovac and at all Ustasha death camps combined and the total number of war dead in Yugoslavia. There are a number that have used not the roles of victims or the hypothesis of the numbers of people which were just -- might have been based on eye witnesses but were instead based on census records. One is by Professor Shajavic. I do not have that citation at hand but it is certainly a number that is much closer to Dr. Tudjman's than those that are frequently used on the Serbian side to characterise those losses. My own conclusions have moved towards the conclusions of Zerjavic and a historian named Kocevic. Those are very close to Dr. Tudjman's conclusions. I would tell you that my views on that have changed probably over the last few years in favour of the most scientific and precise studies that have been done. I believe those numbers put the number of people killed in death camps at somewhere around 125,000 and at Jasenovac somewhat below 100,000, with the total number of war victims just over 1 million. I would emphasise, as he does, that this is -- one war death is a crime and it is not acceptable, but I think it is important also from a historical standpoint to have those accurate numbers and I feel we probably have due to that research in the last four or five years, a much more precise understanding of what those numbers are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to go back to what you repeated today, that the Chetniks and the partisans were two resistance movements against the occupiers against the Nazis. So I'm asking you to mention a battle that the Chetniks waged against the Italians or the Germans.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you a battle name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know whether they fought against the Germans and the Italians as all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By November of 1991 (sic) the Cetnik movement was basically out of the resistance business and it came to numerous agreements both with the occupying powers and even with NDH and attempted to prepare agreements with the partisans on this topic. Your point is, of course, that the Cetnik movement never really mounted an effective resistance. I would say that it had that intention at the beginning of the war but by the end of 1941 had really lost the will to do that and resistance to the occupying forces was left almost exclusively in the hands of the partisans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree with you, but why did you then say that there were two resistance movements if the Cetnik movement was not, in effect, a resistance movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It began that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go on to page 148 and 149, where you spoke about the Germans who organised a Muslim unit. So my question is: the Muslims of the time in Bosnia, did they participate in regular Ustasha units as well outside this one unit organised by the Germans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. My assumption would be that there was at least some of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Muslims held senior posts in the independent state of Croatia? I'm thinking of Pavolic's Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A Muslim was designated as, I think, first deputy Prime Minister or second Prime Minister. There was a Muslim who was appointed to a high position in the independent state of Croatia and there were Muslims appointed to some other positions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know from history the name of Osman Kulenovic, Dzaferbeg Kulenovic, Ademaga Masic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first two you have mentioned I know held positions in the NDH government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When the Ustashas came into power do you know who at that moment was President of the Yugoslav Muslim organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You spoke about inter-ethnic violence from 1941 until the end of the war. When President Tito came into power in Yugoslavia did you encounter any large scale inner ethnic violence after that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was violence. I do not characterise it as inter-ethnic in the sense that one ethnic group was trying to retaliate or exterminate another, but one should certainly note the events of May 1945, when various forces, including Slovene, Croat and even partisan forces and some Serbs were attempting to escape the partisan advance and to flee into Austria the so-called Bleiburg massacres. In that situation the British basically turned these people back into the arms of the partisans and many of them were summarily executed. The number of people killed there is, I think, typically looked at in terms of about 20,000, a substantial number of people. It was a very politically motivated set of killings. It probably doesn't -- you know, although again certainly not to minimise this, but it was not a specifically ethnically or nationally motivated set of killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that 20,000 dead in Bleiburg. Among them how many were Croat victims roughly, among the 20,000 Bleiburg victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not certain. A substantial number of them were Croats and some were Slovenes as well. I think probably the majority from Croats and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Which unit did this in Bleiburg? Where did it come from? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. So we come to Tito's Yugoslavia. You said that Tito's Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, perhaps we could take our break now and you can resume at 11.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are resuming our hearing. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Donia, we said that we would move on to the period of Tito's Yugoslavia. In your examination-in-chief you mentioned that Yugoslavia was a centralised state for the most part during the rule of Joseph Broz Tito; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It began as a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It began as a centralised state modelled after the Soviet constitution of 1936 and very much committed to administrative centralisation. It remained that way through the early 1950s, but some first indications of decentralisation or less stringent central control started emerging already in the years immediately after the break with Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But when would we would be able to mark the time until which Yugoslavia was a centralised state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think there's a particular point in time but rather a progressive decentralisation which achieved institutional status in the constitution of 1974. There were numerous efforts at decentralisation, at reform, at decentralisation, some of which were successful and others not, but I think as a general statement one could look at a process of decentralisation from the early 1950s into the mid-1970s.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that in the constitution of 1974 the decentralisation was institutionalised. I would like to bring you back and ask you to comment how the Communist Party influenced the decentralisation, and I mean by this through its organisation and its -- the influence that it had in the government bodies. Were they contributing to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In order to make things a bit easier, I would ask you to ask clear, specific questions, not too many questions at the same time, one on top of the other, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is a bit complicated. That is, regardless of the constitution, centralised or decentralised, what model of government was introduced by the Communist Party and how did it influence the country? Were the decisions made at the top or were they more grass root?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would distinguish between centralisation, decentralisation, on the one hand, and a single-party state versus pluralism on the other hand. Yugoslavia began as a centralised, single-party state. By the early 1950s it was beginning a gradual uneven process of decentralisation. There remained one political party in Yugoslavia from that time until I would say perhaps right to the end. However, one must recognise that that party became very fragmented along republican lines in the course of even the 1960s, so that the party was a single entity but had republican components, which had very distinct interests and pursued those interests, even as the process of decentralisation was going on, but I would not want to suggest that political pluralism in the sense of a multi-party system entered Yugoslavia prior to the late 1980s or even 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let's try it this way. The JNA, the Yugoslav National Army, were they -- was it a centralised or decentralised institution up until 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav National Army was a centralised institution, one whose leadership up until that time was very committed to the preservation of the Yugoslav state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During the State socialism period, especially during the period of Tito's rule, who controlled the State financial funds? Was it the federation authorities or the republican ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By and large the federal funds were controlled by the federal authorities and those decisions were made by people in power who tended to be high party members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During the period of the state socialism, before the self-government, self-management part, who controlled the highest -- who controlled companies who had the highest profit, that was were they controlled by the federal bodies or by the republican ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you clarify for me what time period you mean by "state socialism"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is before self-management was introduced, before the self-management socialists period. I think we can break up the period of Tito's rule into state socialism and self-management. There is a difference there. So there were state export companies during the State period. Do you know who managed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I would ask you for some year. I think that self-management was introduced in 1949. I can certainly answer for the period of 1945-1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We would -- I would disagree that the self-management was introduced then. I am thinking more of the 1960s?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to whether Mr. Nobilo agrees or disagrees with the witness' answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I sustain this objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's say the 1960s, up until 1956. Let us say from 1945-1965. My question is: who managed the State export companies in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federal Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During this same period who controlled the Federal National Bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federal Government controlled the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you define -- was there the economic equality in Yugoslavia, let's say, up until 1974 and following 1974, the economic equality between the different republics, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until 1974?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think even economists might get in a bar fight over the answer to that question. It's generally viewed by a the supporters of Croatia and Slovenia that those funds were disproportionately awarded to the under-developed republics and I think that probably that is unquestionably the case in accord with the Federal Republic's developmental objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you give us a general assessment of the socialist Yugoslavia? Was there an ethnic equality or did one ethnic group dominate over the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's an "either/or" question and I do not want to really answer "either/or". I think the Federal Republic set out with a strong commitment to national equality between the various nationalities, implemented radical measures to implement that equality, some of which were very successful, others of which were not, and so by the 1970s we see substantial dissatisfaction in certain republics with the allocation of federal resources in particular. However, this was articulated principally in terms of republics rather than between nationalities or ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me which nationality dominated in the Federal bodies, including the military and all the other Federal bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've indicated, I can't answer that question with a straightforward naming you one nationality. I do not accept the premise of your question that one nationality dominated federal institutions throughout the socialist period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, excuse me. Were you talking about republics or nationalities in that last question? The interpretation says: "What was the dominant nationality?". Do you mean what was the dominant republic or was there a dominant republic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At this time I am asking about nationality. That means a nation, an ethnic group. Was it dominating in the federal bodies at this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, I reject your premise that there was a dominant nationality in federal bodies throughout the period of Socialist Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So could you give us like a general assessment about the Socialist Yugoslavia? Was it a democratic country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a very value-laden term, and it's difficult to assess it throughout the period. I believe that the Federal Republic became more democratic as time went along in that the party became more wider -- there was greatest participation in party organs. Internal disputes within the party became over time more open. So I would be -- to my understanding of democracy, I would say there was a gradual movement towards a more democratic society. However, this remained a one party state throughout the period of Socialist Yugoslavia, one in which there were central institutions that would not tolerate secession or pluralist movements. That is an intrinsic part of my understanding of democracy. Thus I would have to give you a qualified answer. I think there was a gradual tend towards more democratisation in the period of socialist Yugoslavia, but it never fully became a democratic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the status or the protection of human rights in the socialist Yugoslavia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it at times was better than others. By "human rights" again there are various understandings. There was no question that the rights of individuals were violated from time to time and at times frequently by the Yugoslav Secret Police in various episodes and incidents. It was certainly a much better human rights environment than in any socialist country that I could think of in the Eastern Bloc. So again, relatively speaking, there were several human rights violations and, not to be overlooked, but as a generalisation, this became a much more tolerant environment than was typical of west European countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Maybe if I asked you specifically. Would a person who tended to express their opinions that were not in accordance with the generally accepted rules with the constitution be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I was there on numerous occasions in the 1960s and 1970s and people expressed to me very openly their political views. To my knowledge they were not prosecuted for those views. There were certainly instances in which people were prosecuted for political activities in support of or in promotion of those views.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to move to page 154 of the transcript, where you talked about motivation for decentralisation by Joseph Broz Tito, who was preparing a successor. You said that he did not want to be succeeded by another strong personality. What would be the motives of Joseph Broz Tito that led him to promulgate the constitutional views of 1974?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think you have just identified the primary motivation, which was perhaps a certain paranoia on Tito's part that he would be succeeded by some strong man with policies that were contrary to what his personal policies and views were. He clearly hoped that the constitution as a decentralising element would allow all the political contenders within Yugoslavia to maximise their freedom of political activity and economic development under the general umbrella of the federal structure. He believed that this decentralised system would in some manner work. Indeed, it did for some period of time after his death, but the destabilising component within it was, I think, obvious to many observers already in 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In other words, was the principal motivation a personal jealousy or was it an attempt to rescue Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think you can remove his personal experiences from that policy. He had turned to various people in hopes that they would succeed him and been disappointed in their eagerness to seize power or to assume power, and so I do not think that one should remove his personal experience from that determination. He certainly hoped that Yugoslavia would out last him, would survive him, and his -- I view the 1974 constitution as his final legacy. It in many respects did optimise the freedom of movement of the republics and at the same time it failed to provide a succession structure which would be durable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm moving to when the tensions started rising in Bosnia. The Agrocomerc affair, the victims in Neum. I would like to know who were the victims of these affairs. The political representatives of which nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think in general the victims were members of the older political establishment and certainly there was victims of the movements from a wide array of political leadership. My impression is that the Muslim leaders probably suffered principally in Dizdarevic's removal from succession to the Presidency and in general the Muslim political leadership probably got the worst of this. It was, however, a generation movement in that the socialist alliance was what was driving it, or at least the latter parts of it, rather than a nationalist coup of some sort in the Bosnian party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You talked about the socialist youth and you mentioned socialist alliance. Who spearheaded this movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was the Socialist Youth Alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Last time you said -- you mentioned the Socialist Youth and the investigative journalist. My question to you: do you really believe that there were investigative journalists in the Socialist Yugoslavia and that the Socialist Youth was an independent group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are two questions there. Were there independent investigative journalists in Yugoslavia? Yes, absolutely. One can identify the papers that they worked for. Borba became one; Nasidani in Bosnia. Investigative journalism actually can be dated to the 1970s, when there was some aggressive reporting on bankruptcies and other economic issues. So investigative journalism has, in fact, an important role in the development of a more open approach to political questions dating back some years. As to your question of whether the Socialist Youth Alliance was independent, I would say again I would hesitate to characterise it as either a slave of the broader party or fully independent. I think it emerged as a force with some autonomy in the course of the late 1980s at the same time that other youth movements of younger party members, such as Mladost in Slovenia, this was taking place in other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The persons that were victims of these affairs, you said that they were mostly Muslims. How do you perceive them, as Muslims who wanted more decentralisation, or do you perceive them as Muslim politicians who wanted more centralisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is again a complicated answer. I would prefer to say I just do not know. I think that the issues for Bosnia were somewhat different than the issues for Yugoslavia. Within the Bosnia party there were some questions of party coherence, pluralism versus unitary party organisation and within Yugoslavia there was clearly a question of the role of the Bosnian Muslims in the federal institutions, particularly the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Within the framework of such political relationships persons who were victims in these affairs, what did they advocate? Which concept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, I can't give you a simple answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your general assessment why did the Socialist Yugoslavia break up? What are the causes of its break-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a very important and very complicated question. I think there are numerous answers to it. The one was first clearly the erosion of central institutions. That erosion had obviously actors pressing forward in it. The seizure of power in the Communist Party of Serbia by Milosevic I feel was a prime cause of the break-up, not immediately, but had far-reaching ramifications. Certainly the changing role of the Yugoslav National Army played an important role as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you give us a chronology of events that signified the break-up of Yugoslavia with the perspective of several years now, in other words particular specific events that marked the gradual break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already tried to do that with some events, and I'm sure that I have omitted many, but would not know exactly where to go to fill in that process further than I've done it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you be more -- remember, Mr. Nobilo, that the witness gave us a sketch of an entire chronology. I am not sure that this cannot be clarified -- will clarify anything if you ask him by memory. If you ask him to repeat the chronology of events, starting with the document you have, which is one of the exhibits, you might be able to say whether -- I do not want to tell you what questions to ask but maybe you could supplement or ask him a comment on certain dates that needed to be added but to ask once again for a chronology which the witness already presented in the documents seems a bit difficult to me and also might be a reason -- might be a waste of time, in fact. Would you re-ask the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I shall try to put the question in a different way. How do you assess the gathering at Gazimaston? When was it held and what is the import of that gathering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My next question: do you know anything about the miners' strike in Kosovo, when they were on strike in the pits underground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There certainly were strikes in Kosovo. I think there were strikes in 1980 and again in 1989. I'm sorry. I just do not know where you're going with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Namely I'm interested in the nature of that strike. Were the demands of those miners underground of a political nature or purely of a social nature as a labour strike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would characterise that movement as both economic and political.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the events of the people in Kosovo under the leadership of Miroslav Solevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the popular events in Montenegro, when there was a change of power under the influence of the demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think you just summarised it. There was indeed a change of power under the influence of demonstrations organised under Milosevic's leadership. I can't give you the precise date, but I believe it was in late 1988 or early 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But what were the main demands of the demonstrators, their political demands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were demanding the resignation of the political leadership of the League of Communists of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But why did they demand their resignation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was part of demonstrations that took place in Montenegro, in Vojvodina and attempted demonstrations in Slovenia and in Kosovo to install party leaders who were loyal to Milosevic. The existing party leadership was -- again it is kind of the same issues that arose in Bosnia -- viewed as old, as ineffective and as not sufficiently vital and self-interested in the general nature of the economic situation. So I would put those events in the context of an effort by Milosevic-inspired crowds to force the resignation of the Communist Party -- league of communist leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you say what you feel regarding the demonstrators that wanted Milosevic supporters to come into power? Were they extreme nationalists or were they not so extremist, or, rather, could you put within that context the change of power in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were principally people who were given a day off, a bus ride and a lunch to participate in the demonstrations, and it's difficult to characterise their politics much beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you perhaps be more specific regarding the slogans that were most frequently used in view of the nationalism in Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From Milosevic, the pro-Milosevic people were motivated by the notion of an anti-bureaucratic revolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You'd have to ask them. I would say it is a slogan that has utterly no meaning to most of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you assess that movement demanding an anti-bureaucratic revolution as a movement of Serb nationalists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned in passing something, but was a similar movement in Vojvodina the one that toppled the existing authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened in Ljubljana with this anti-bureaucratic movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A demonstration was scheduled for Ljubljana and the demonstrators were to arrive from the east by trains and to avoid this demonstration from taking place, with the obvious undesirable consequences from the point of view of the Slovene political leadership, they simply shut down the railroads and the roads. Subsequently those demonstrators were unable to gather in Ljubljana and the demonstration never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me in general terms regarding this anti-bureaucratic revolution in what year was it operative? When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned 1988 and 1989. It has remained a slogan of Milosevic for some time after that, but he came to power in the Serbian party in 1987. That is certainly a date that I identify as the first time in which the use of crowds, mobs, tried to force a change in the constitutional structure in Yugoslavia, and therefore represented a departure from accepted norms of contention within the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know something about the economic embargo enforced by Serbia against Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The economic embargo followed upon this demonstrate or scheduled demonstration that we have talked about and was an effort to force the Slovene leadership to its knees in economic terms. Slovenia was sufficiently economically independent so that this did not have its desired consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me what is the importance of the 14th extraordinary congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia held in January 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I indicated, I believe, in my direct testimony, this was the congress labelled "extraordinary", because it was hoped that this congress would resolve the outstanding constitutional issues in Yugoslavia and provide some constitutional mechanism or compromise mechanism to allow the party to stay together. At that meeting the proceedings failed to yield that result and the Slovenian delegation walked out of the meeting followed closely by the Croatian delegation. Subsequently the session was adjourned indefinitely. Within a period of two or three weeks this effectively spelled the end of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia as a functioning, centralised institution. It clearly was severely weakened going into this meeting, and this is normally the date that is credited with its -- the date on which its demise was final.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
