utterances.text: As far as I have been able to understand, after that event the congress was never continued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us anything about the memorandum, which you did not mention, of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, what it was and what its importance was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like many documents, it has probably assumed more importance to those who reacted to it since then than those who originally wrote it, but it was a document, a draft document prepared by certain members of the Academy of Sciences, the Serbian Academy of Sciences, which listed a series of complaints about Serbian disadvantages in the Federal Republic and complained that the Serbs were discriminated against in various ways in Federal Yugoslavia. It subsequently gained great notoriety as a document espousing greater Serbian nationalism. There certainly was that element in it, but I think the language is much more moderate and its topic is much more moderate than some people made it out to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you indicate when the memorandum was published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was published in 19 -- it was drafted in 1986. It was published a couple of months, I believe, after it was drafted, and I can't give you the month. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the western Serbian borders as interpreted by Vuk Draskovic, Miroslav Solevic and Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are three different questions there, I believe. I can tell you that in the opinion of all of those people the claims of Serbia in their minds were such that Serbian territory should reach far to the west of where The Republic of Serbia's borders were, not a complete disagreement on either, but they all clearly claimed Bosnia portions of Croatia and generally favoured a far westward extension of the boundaries that you are speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we say regarding the most significant politician among them, Vuk Draskovic, how he designated the western borders of Serbia? Which towns did he indicate as marking those borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Stipe Mesic and the problems surrounding his election as President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation which Tito had left in the constitution of 1974 was such that upon his death there would be a rotation in the members of the Presidency and, in fact, as time went along, the succession was determined years in advance. There was a nominal vote of confirmation as each one of these one-year successions took place after Tito's death in May of 1980, and on May 15th of 1991 Stipe Mesic was next in line to succeed to the President of the Presidency. By that time the coup -- coups in Montenegro, Vojvodina and Kosovo had taken place, so that four of the eight votes on the Presidency were essentially under the control of Milosevic: going into that meeting there was a strenuous effort to get an agreement to confirm Mesic, who was really believed by many people to be a devoted Croatian nationalist, and the vote ultimately came to 4 to 4. At that point the Federal Presidency as such ceased to exist in the minds of most legal experts. At that time -- this was May of 1991 -- just as the events in Croatia and Slovenia were starting to unfold and consequently the international community became involved, and a part of the compromise that came out of the discussions about Slovenia resulted in an agreement that Mesic would be confirmed as the President of the Presidency, and that took place, I believe, in July of 1991. He held that position for about five or six months, I believe, resigned in December, if I'm not mistaken, but was -- had very little effect in that role as President of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If we put aside all you have said about Mesic, all the other events through memorandum, the popular meetings in Kosovo, Vojvodina, Montenegro and Ljubljana, was this before or after Tudjman came into power in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tudjman came into power in the course of 1990, so the developments that you are speaking of were principally prior to his assuming office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How could we describe the year 1990, the moment when Tudjman came into office, in relation to the functioning of the federal bodies and inter-ethnic relations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do not understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tudjman came into power in 1990 so my question is: could you briefly describe or define the conditions under which he came into power in relation to, first, the functioning of federal bodies and, secondly, in relation to ethnic relationships in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me try the first question first. He came into power in accord with the elections that were held in each republic in the course of 1990. It was widely planned that there would be a federal election in that year and that election was never held. Consequently there were elections in each republic and by 1990 these republics were functioning very substantially autonomously. What federal institutions there were were very weakened with the exception of the Yugoslav National Army. So I think one could say that Tudjman's coming to power in 1990 took place at a time when the republics were almost on their own in terms of the practical day-to-day running of affairs but still had serious business to transact with the Federal Republic and the Croatian and Slovenian sides were clearly seeking to avoid the -- they were fearful, if you will, of the exercise of federal authority as it was being practised by Milosevic. Your second question was in terms of ethnic relations, and I would only say that although some of the parties that won in various republics were, in fact, communists, that all candidates who won, including Tudjman, did so on a nationalist platform, and so the ethnic dimension of things was clearly moving in a very nationalist direction at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. So we come to page 167 of the transcript and certain citations that you made from Tudjman's book, and reading that book as a whole, did you anywhere come across Tudjman advocating a violent change of borders by war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tudjman in that work, does he anywhere underline or disseminate nationalist hatred towards any nation and specifically towards the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that work, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In that work does he advocate forcible movements of populations, resettlement of populations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he does not in that work. He has taken positions in other works which indicate that he is -- as a kind of a moral or philosophical issue views certain types of violence as a deeply ingrained part of, let's say, historical movements. However, in this particular work I do not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When we are talking about violence, does he instigate violence at the present time or does he explain it in history?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me read a statement from his new book, which is: "The horrors of war" in which he states as follows: "Common military violence is transformed into genocidal extermination and deportation of populations when the conqueror has permanent designs upon the territory and ethnic assimilation of the opposing nations". I must say that that comes very close to an advocacy position. It certainly states that it is deeply ingrained in the character of military violence when annexationist aims are at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He explains the concept, but does he favour such action now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He does not specifically advocate a course of action in a particular situation, no. He is speaking from the kind of philosophical, historical standpoint here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the attitude of the Republic of Croatia was towards The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding its borders? Has Croatia recognised those borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have indicated, I think The Republic of Croatia has followed two different tracks in its approach to Bosnia. The first, which is premised on some sort of a military alliance with Bosnia, was followed on April 7th, 1992 with a recognition and with the various international communities' involvement in Croatian matters. At the same time it's clear that in action in terms of establishing the Herceg-Bosna area that those borders have not been respected in terms of the actual policies of the Croatian Republic towards Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have now reached pages 167, 168 and 169, where you quoted elements from the mentioned book of Franjo Tudjman. So I should like to throw some light on those allegations of his and to hear your views on them. Do you agree with Franjo Tudjman's statement that Serbia and Vojvodina had strong historical, national, economic and cultural links, Serbia and Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's true. Again I would want to clarify the period of history at which that has been true. It has been true at some times more than others but certainly say for the period 1690 strengthened those ties for a couple of decades after 1690 and at various times they have been strong, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go on to some other statements you made yesterday, quoting from his book. The next one, do you think that is correct, that large parts of Croatia were attached to Bosnia only after Turkey's occupation? Is that correct historically speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I perhaps should go to the transcript, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is page 169, line 17: "Large parts of Croatia had been incorporated into Bosnia by the Turks"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Page 169, line 17. (Pause.)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I think it's a statement that has to be carefully interpreted. It is in part fully true, but one could easily extend the definition of Croatia to points that I think would be questionable. So clearly large parts of what had been Croatia were incorporated into the military frontier, and I would say perhaps some parts of Croatia, but I would maybe not want to agree that large parts had been incorporated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the notion of Turkish Croatia, the western part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did that part of Bosnia become a component part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think you've said it yourself. It has been so for a long time. If you are speaking of Jajce and Bihac, you know Jajce was the ancient capital for some time and I think it has certainly been part of Bosnia for many centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I was thinking of Bihac and western Bosnia which is known as Turkish Croatia. So when did that part become part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it became part of Bosnia in the course of the Ottoman administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Another statement is contained in the following sentence, and that is that: "Bosnia and Herzegovina were historically linked to Croatia and also geographically and economically linked". Is that allegation of Franjo Tudjman as a historian correct in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. In your view, the shape of Croatia, the one it has now, is that a customary shape for a state, or is it some kind of an exception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of no customary shape for a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know any other state that looks like that or is anything like that in shape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not visualising all hundreds of states in the world in my mind right now, but I would say that it is -- there is no customary shape for a state. They assume very different dimensions, depending on natural features, depending on historical boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The question in the referendum in the Republic of Croatia on 19th May, do you know what it was, what was the question put to the referendum in May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 19th May 1991 a referendum was held in Croatia and there was a question put to the electorate, to which they had to answer "yes" or "no", so I'm asking you whether you know what the question was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I believe that was the date of the Croatian referendum on independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But what was the contents of the question? What do the people have to declare themselves in favour of? Was it an independent Croatia or a Croatia that would link with the federal state in the form of a confederation; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know whether the question put to the referendum contained any reference to the attitude towards the Serbian minority in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, it's now 1 o'clock. Perhaps we could stop, but I would also like to ask you if you could tell us about how long you still have, either you or Mr. Hayman, for the cross-examination. I'm asking only the question so that we can organise our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I think it will not take more than an hour as far as I'm concerned, but Mr. Hayman will continue after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have probably two hours of questions. That's my best guess, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point, your Honour, this is going to be a double cross-examination, and the Prosecutor would strenuously object to this practice of double cross-examination. Now I need not remind the court that Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Hayman have had two weeks, actually more than two weeks, your Honour now -- almost three weeks since June 25th 1997 until today to prepare for this cross-examination. Now taken to its logical conclusion, the cross-examination of every defence witness could, of course, be done by the three of us in turn. The Prosecutor has made a commitment that we will do single cross-examinations. Now the last cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What are you suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I suggest at this point that Mr. Hayman be precluded and be prevented from cross-examining Mr. Donia, and Mr. Nobilo finish the cross-examination from beginning to end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The judges will decide that and we will resume our hearing at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Registrar, please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We stopped this morning on an issue raised by the Prosecutor. The Trial Chamber has decided as follows. From now on -- yes, please come in. The witness may come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: On behalf of my colleagues I wanted to respond to the question which was raised by the Prosecutor at the point that we suspended our hearing. The Trial Chamber has decided that whenever a witness is called to testify, he may be cross-examined or examined by one counsel. Number two, it happens that this principle perhaps was not expressed clearly, because about two weeks ago we proceeded differently at the time that there was another witness testifying. At that time or under those conditions it is, of course, legitimate that Mr. Hayman worked together with Mr. Nobilo and prepared to make an intervention. Therefore, the Trial Chamber has now decided that for the last time today two lawyers will be able to speak during the cross-examination, but this -- let me finish, Mr. Hayman, please -- but this will be the second time and the last time. From this time forward there will only be one witness, one interrogation, one cross-examination each by one lawyer, and the Trial Chamber would like that the questioning of the witness be concluded this afternoon, because the judges themselves have certain questions they would like to ask. I see that Mr. Hayman wants to make a comment and I now give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Briefly, your Honour, we would have liked to have been heard on this matter, simply because although we do not expect it necessary in the case of many witnesses to seek both the opportunity for both Mr. Nobilo and myself to cross-examine the witness, there are -- will be some witnesses, like this witness, whose expertise in testimony falls between two languages, between two worlds, if you will. Mr. Nobilo has a special knowledge of the history of the Balkans, knowledge from growing up in Yugoslavia. His father fought with the partisans, knowledge I cannot gain through weeks of study. At the same time Mr. Nobilo's English, although workable, he cannot read English with any speed. I think I am safe in saying that without insulting my colleague. This witness, while he speaks Serbo-Croatian, Bosnian, and he has worked in that culture and on that subject matter he has written and published voluminously in English. To ask Mr. Nobilo to digest those materials and conduct the cross-examination I submit would not be appropriate. I do not want to slow down the proceedings, but I would ask that the court leave open the possibility that there may be future witnesses, perhaps the exception, not the rule, where to require either Mr. Nobilo or myself to conduct the entire examination would work an extreme hardship on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The answer to that quite clearly is that counsel has made a choice. Now I personally read English probably as well or maybe not as well as Mr. Hayman, but he could have gone out in the last three weeks and purchased Mr. Donia's book and participated and done the examination himself and consulted with any number of people. The issue quite clearly here is that the Defence seeks to have two shots at prosecution witnesses and they have had three weeks to prepare this cross-examination of this particular gentleman. Now in the spirit of moving this matter along I think that the trial court should continue with your Honours' -- Mr. President's and your Honours' ruling that Mr. Hayman and Mr. Nobilo take one shot on cross-examination and that's it. Now if taken to its logical conclusion, if we talk about expertise, I am sure Mr. Hayman and Mr. Cayley have expertise in areas I do not have expertise in and various subject matters. I do not know what's going to come up in this case. However, there has to be a line drawn at a point where the protracted cross-examination has to end and this is the point. I ask the court most respectfully to continue to the court's ruling, to just permit one cross-examination and not permit this double team by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard you, but will not change its decision, Mr. Hayman. It refers to two points. There must have been a misunderstanding at the beginning. I am certainly responsible for it and I ask your pardon for that, but the Presiding Judge with his two colleagues has tried to work in such a way that there be a certain kind of order and equity that would be as perfect as possible during the hearing. That is why today only, because you were not advised, you, Mr. Hayman, can speak. As for the rest, it is a question of good organisation and I believe that the Trial Chamber even if it seems to be pushing you a bit, it does generally leave you the time to organise yourself and I think you simply have to organise yourselves amongst yourselves. This is also applicable to the Prosecution. Aside from this afternoon, since you didn't know what the rules were, you may speak but into the future I want the rules to be very clear. When a witness comes to testify, he will be questioned only by one person from the Office of the Prosecutor and cross-examined by one member of the Defence team. This is being done in the interests of justice so the trial moves forward as quickly as possible, as harmoniously and equitably as possible. The question has now been resolved and I can give the floor back to Mr. Nobilo to continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor Donia, could you please go to page 171 of the transcript, because I have a very specific question and I would like you to be able to refer to it? Page 171.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Line 7, starting -- this is from Mr. Tudjman's book, where he says that: "In the Croatian Banovina the Croats had a clear majority". Is that correct? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Further, you gave the data on how many Croat -- what was the size of Croatian population in each of the kotars that went into the Banovina. Then on the following page, lines 3-7, you draw a conclusion that the Croats had the majority only if they had also included the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question to you now is the following: is it correct to say, when talking about the historian Tudjman, that the Croats had a majority in Banovina when citing the census report from 1991, when you referred to the census of 1939 in reference to the Croatian Banovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reference that I made here is to the census figures from 1991. I do not believe there was a census in 1939. There was one earlier in the 1930s, I believe 1931, and I do not have those figures available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you believe that it is correct to use those -- that information, those data? The Croats may have gained a majority in the meantime. What do you think on that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have looked at the 1910 census, which shows a remarkable consistency in percentage of the Catholic population in those districts with the numbers that I have given here. So while I concur that this is a long stretch of time, 81 years, with 1939 something in the middle, your point is well taken that my numbers here are not taken from the nearest census to the creation of the Banovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you then withdraw your conclusion that Tudjman was thinking that the Muslims should be incorporated so that the Croats would gain a clear majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. He clearly goes on in his explanation to argue that the Muslims are Croats, and it is only using that kind of logic that this argument can be advanced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And can you tell us when he said that the Croats were in the majority, did he also have Muslims in mind or were the Croats actually in the majority in 1939?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the quote that you have here on lines 7 through 12 is in the English language version in the present tense. This is a book published in 1981. So his statement that: "The Croats have a clear majority", clearly pertains to a time period later than the 1939 agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Correct. However, your comment was that the Croats were not in the majority. They were in the majority in 1939 only including the Muslims, but now my question to you is whether you would allow that the Croats themselves, without the Muslims, were the majority in these kotars, in these counties, in 1939?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am open to that evidence, but have not seen any evidence that would lead me to conclude that they were in 1939. I would note again that there were some plans for plebiscites that were discussed in the negotiations prior to the 1939 agreement. Those plebiscites were never held, because the agreement was sealed rather quickly in the course of these negotiations. So my conclusion is that I simply have no basis for believing that the Croats were in a majority in these particular districts in 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am pointing to your inference, 181 page: "No counties have a Croatian majority. The only way to get these numbers is to include in these six counties the Muslim population in addition to the Croatian". However, you do not have the data, so you cannot draw any inferences if you do not have the population data, the census data for these six counties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I've said, I have looked at 1991. I have also looked at 1910. The percentages are remarkably similar. Looking at the religious data, I feel that's a conclusion I can reach. I am open to other data that may contradict it, but I see no reason to abandon the conclusion that one can only get to a majority, that is an absolute majority, in these counties by grouping together the Croats and the Muslims. This is not the case in Herzegovina where there are several kotars or counties in which there was an absolute Muslim majority, but in reference to these Bosnian districts, it seems to me that it's highly unlikely that in 1939 one can come to the conclusion that there was a majority of Croats in each of these districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, thank you. In any event we can conclude that you do not have data for 1939; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We'll move on. You talked about the positions of Mr. Tudjman in his history books. Can you tell us something about his personal views as a politician on the issue of the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I fail to distinguish in many respects between his role as a historian and as a politician. I think that he has been remarkably consistent in implementing certain of his views reached as a historian in his role as a politician as well. I guess I don't have any insight into what his personal views might be apart from those expressed by him as a historian and writer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Alija Izetbegovic's preparedness to accept the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you give me a time period in which you would like to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 16th September 1993 the agreement between Izetbegovic and Krajisnik mediated by Messrs. Stoltenberg and Owen, where there was a provision that The Republic could be divided after two years. Do you know anything about this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that specific agreement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you have any information on whether any international factors, as they were called in the former Yugoslavia, were advocating the division -- the United States, Germany, Great Britain, United Nations, one of the five big agreements that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think one should look at this as a series of proposals which involve to a greater or lesser extent the separation of parts of Bosnia. In the discussions that took place under the European community in February and March of 1992, there was, of course, much discussion of cantonisation, and I think that all of the parties viewed that as an almost idyllic resolution on the Swiss model rather than a plan for outright partition, but as time went along and these discussions came under the leadership of the London conference in the summer of 1992 and led to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, these became much more closer to what one would characterise as partition. President Izetbegovic was involved in these discussions from the very beginning. At various times he agreed to different proposals for the separation of Bosnia into component parts, including the cantonisation proposal that was first proposed in Lisbon and subsequently to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. So I think he was involved in these discussions from the very beginning, and right up through the Dayton peace agreements there were on-going discussions about the resolutions that would allow a peaceful end of the conflict and virtually every one of those proposals involved some form of division. At the same time President Izetbegovic frequently asserted in the language of the United Nations' resolutions his belief in a politically independent sovereign and united Bosnia and Herzegovina. These two in a sense were in some conflict. They were in conflict not only in terms of the policy that Mr. Izetbegovic pursued, but also that the policy that was being pursued by the international community. The United Nations' resolutions were asserting one thing and at the same time the Vance-Owen talks were clearly leading to some form of division.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we conclude that during the negotiations which was meant to resolve the war situation in Bosnia, all the participants had in mind or operated with certain modes of division within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one time or another I believe that is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please move on? You mentioned five major peace agreements in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would like to take you from one to the -- through all of them so that we can see what the form of the central and regional government was. That means the division of power between the ethnic constituent parts and the central government, for instance, of 23rd February 1993, the Gutiero plan of the EU. Can you define these provisions just briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not going to be able to address issues of constitutional law in this regard, but I can generally characterise the agreement of the Gutiero plan or agreement from Lisbon as one which supported cantonisation and, as I've said, I think that the cantonisation that people had in mind was the establishment of political units which were largely self-contained but which had nevertheless a strong participation in the central government. If you wish to move on to the provisions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a moment. I apologise. The EU plan of Lisbon, can you tell us who signed it and who did not sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was signed in Sarajevo on March 18th. I believe it was signed by all parties, the Bosnian Croat party, President Izetbegovic for the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The logical question that arises from it: why wasn't it implemented? Would you know an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The agreement was renounced by President Izetbegovic shortly after he signed it, towards the end of the month of March, and it was also, I would note, a rather desperate last minute effort to reach a negotiated settlement when other developments on the ground were rapidly leading to a military confrontation and, in fact, skirmishes had already broken out in parts of Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Between which sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next as you mentioned in examination-in-chief the Vance-Owen plans from January 1993. Can you give us the main characteristics of this plan and who signed it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen plan was an outcome from the London conference of August 1992, which asserted certain constitutional -- certain principles for a peace plan, including the return of the right of all refugees to return to their homes, and then went on to specify some provisional agreements, ultimately a demilitarisation and some constitutional provisions. These protracted negotiations in the Fall of 1992 really did not lead to a consensus or an agreement by the three parties on a map in particular. As I indicated in my direct testimony on January 3rd, 1993, Mate Boban signed the Vance-Owen plan in its entirety on behalf of the Croats. Then on March 25th, after three long sessions in New York Alija Izetbegovic signed on behalf of the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Serbs, although at one point the agreement was initialled by Radovan Karadzic on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs, it was never, in fact, endorsed by the assembly of the Bosnian Serbs and therefore never effectively ratified by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened to Alija Izetbegovic's position, that is his signature? Did he abide by his commitment to the agreement or did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The agreement was never concluded because the Bosnian Serbs never completed their ratification of it. President Izetbegovic indicated at the time of signing and in the several days after signing the document that he would withdraw his signature within a period of ten to fifteen days if the international community did not succeed in persuading the Bosnian Serbs to ratify the agreement or did not employ force to assure its implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And did he -- did his signature stay on this agreement or did he withdraw it -- I mean Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, he never withdrew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you address the relationship between the central government and the provincial governments? According to the Vance-Owen plan, what would be the relationship between the central and local government, the provincial governments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were ten provincial governments stated or outlined and the relationship between the central government and each of these provincial entities was to be quite weak. The central government would have responsibility for foreign policy and some administrative matters, but most other items would be left to the individual provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. The next plan you mention was the agreement between the Croats and Muslims from March 1994. This was the fourth major plan, if I recall correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we skipped number 3. Just very briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Correct. The Owen-Stoltenberg from June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, there were a number of successive plans which fall under the category of the Owen-Stoltenberg agreement -- mediation and none of them were quite the same. There was the union of republics; there was the so-called proposal that was reached in the British cruiser in the Adriatic Sea, which was from September of 1993; these and a couple of other plans which are essentially territorial modifications of the Vance-Owen plan were considered and for one reason or another not ratified by all three parties in the course of the latter half of 1993. Actually I would say the months from June until early January 1994 -- June of 1993 until early January of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The common denominator of all these plans is the existence of republics within Bosnia-Herzegovina and a view of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a union of republics, all this in reference to the Owen-Stoltenberg plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree that that is one common characteristic and the other common characteristic was the very difficult negotiations intended to give the Bosnian government either initially 30 per cent of the territorial area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a number that later changed to 33 per cent. This was a percentages gain in territorial terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know who signed these Owen-Stoltenberg plans? Who signed all of them? Can you specify which side signed what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I really can't specify what each one did. There was opposition from Izetbegovic to signing at least a couple of those, including the intrepid -- not intrepid -- the plan from the Adriatic cruiser and there was also resistance, of course, to the union of Serb republics, as it was proposed in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you say whether the Croatian side signed these plans, and I mean the Owen-Stoltenberg plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They certainly signed -- I know that they signed the first two, the first one that came in July of 1993 and then the September plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now plan number 4 was the plan from March of 1994. Can you tell us what this plan involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was -- this marked the first direct involvement by United States diplomats to try to create an agreement and resulted in the creation of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina by virtue of an agreement between the Croat and Muslim parties. It began with the so-called Washington accords and subsequently led to -- it began with a cease-fire really between the Croat and Muslim sides and led eventually to a constitutional arrangement which was contained in the Washington agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just in brief, did both sides sign this agreement and kept their signatures on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed they did. Dr Tudjman at the time that he signed gave an unmistakable signal that he was being forced to sign it by the western powers. He stated in the press conference after his signature that: "The west has concluded and is convincing us that we must work together with the Muslims in Bosnia".

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But, if I understood you correctly, all sides signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim and Croats signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of course, yes. Now we move to the Dayton Agreement. Can you tell us in brief what was the division of power between the central government and the government -- the power of the entities and then who all signed this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's probably a question that no-one has quite answered yet, but I'll give you at least an overview answer of how the sovereignty was divided. The Dayton agreements did involve a map that divided Bosnia into two entities, one entity that of the Serb republic and the second entity that of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A central government linking these two entries was to be -- was established with very weak powers and again more of a co-ordinating role than any extensive functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So according to the Dayton accords which are still in effect, how do you assess Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a federation, confederation or union of states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is some combination of all those. It is a weak central polity made up of two largely separate entities, each of which has committed itself to certain principles that are contained in the Dayton agreement, including the rights of refugees to return to their homes, the maintenance of a military balance of power amongst the two entities and a federation which was essentially a non-starter from the beginning and in which the two component parts have very little functioning common life. It's hard to describe that in any short, encapsulated form. The constitutional provisions of the Dayton Agreement are sufficiently complex so that I do not know that I can characterise it in a single phrase or word.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If we review all five of these agreements and a great deal of time spent in negotiating them, am I correct in saying that the basis of all those negotiations was a bargaining over territory? I put it rather bluntly, but maybe an exchange of territories between the entities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They involve several issues. They involved from the very beginning constitutional issues, the relationship between the various component parts. All were established on the basis of United Nations' resolutions and proclamations, which emphasised the political integrity, independence and territorial unit of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They all involved discussions of the provisional arrangements, namely the transitional arrangements which would lead to peace, and a map as well. So I think these negotiations all involved all of those issues, and the one that ultimately prevailed, of course, was the Dayton peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you believe that the acceptance of maps was the main stumbling block, or was it some other constitutional provisions, if we view all these five agreements together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think there were several important issues, and much of the individual discussions centred on maps, but at a number of points in time constitutional arrangements proved to be a more difficult issue to resolve than one might assume. So I would believe that the several issues were involved in these talks and to view them as a map issue alone is an oversimplification of the way these talks proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the Vance-Owen plan and all the other plans that followed, leading up finally to the Washington agreements and the Dayton accords, did the acceptance of that plan mean agreeing to the abolition of Herceg-Bosna? Therefore, the adoption of that plan does it implicitly apply to the abolition of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't conclude -- I'm not a constitutional lawyer and I do not know that I would agree that it does or doesn't lead to the dissolution of Herceg-Bosna. I know that at a number of points in the progression of discussions the Croatian Republic committed itself to the abolition of Herceg-Bosna and I honestly can't give you the dates, but there were several occasions on which that commitment was made, and, of course, not carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to go back a little to page 177, lines 4-7, of the transcript, when you quoted Lord Owen's book, "the Balkan Odyssey", where he says that: "Tudjman carried his nationalism openly on his sleeve and that he had one goal in life, to control the territory which he believed historically belonged to Croatia". A couple of lines above that the period of 1992 and 1993 is mentioned as the year when Mr. Owen described Tudjman in this way. So could you briefly describe the military situation that President Tudjman or Croatia found itself in in 1992 and 1993, the military situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, The Republic of Croatia, of course, was, as I indicated in my direct testimony, involved in a bloody war in the course of 1991, which resulted in a cease-fire and establishment of a United Nations' mandate in the Republic of Croatia. I'm not a military specialist and I would only say that from the point of view of the political developments that I watched, this was a time in Croatia in which perhaps the primary domestic political agenda was building up Croatia's armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the UNPA zones were formed when the UN arrived? What percentage of the territory was under the control of the rebel Croatian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1992, when the United Nations' forces came to the UNPA zone, as we called it, what percentage of the territory at the beginning of 1992 was under the control of the JNA and the Serbian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm unable to give you a percentage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your main position, and please correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Donia, is that Bosnia for centuries was a multi-cultural society and that there were no conflicts among its ethnic groups. So my question is: the nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina before 1991, did they ever independently control their territory without the supervision of some external force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say I think you have not accurately represented my general view on the history of Bosnia. I do not portray it as an idyllic world where no contention occurred. I have made the point that violence, ethnic violence, was largely absent in Bosnia except for two major periods in its history, one in the period 1941-1945, and the second one the period that began in 1992. There was contention, disagreement and plenty of other types of conflict, social, economic and at times one sees the political organisations of the various nationalities working in coalition with one another, breaking up and working with other coalitions. So I do not believe that I have asserted a conflict-free society. I have suggested that the nature of violence in Bosnia's history was largely not of an ethnic character but these other characters. With that clarification, may I ask you if you could re-ask the question so that I can answer you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the history of Bosnia before 1991 was there a period when the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina decided their destiny themselves; in other words, when Bosnia was not a component part of a larger entity, a kingdom or a State?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just say that the term "deciding their destiny by themselves" is a different question from whether they were part of a larger entity. The answer to the first part of that question is yes, I think they had substantial control over their own destinies at various times, but they were, as to the second part of your question, consistently part of some other entity, with the exception of the period of the Medieval Bosnian State, which owed only nominal suzerainty to the Hungarian Crown. After that, of course, Bosnia was part of the Ottoman occupation until 1878; Austro-Hungary, 1878 to 1918. I would say at times at least in that period Bosnians had considerable control over their own destiny, not as much as they wanted to, but then part of the Yugoslav State, part of the independent State of Croatia and then part of Socialist Yugoslavia thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go according to chronology. In what way or partially at least could it decide its destiny during the Ottoman Empire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you asked me if the peoples of Bosnia could decide their own destiny and I think that, first of all, there was a Muslim political elite which gained considerable ability to control its own destiny in the course of early 19th century -- late 18th, early 19th century in Bosnia until some of those movements were crushed by the Ottomans. Certainly at times the Serbian Orthodox institutions in Bosnia had a limited timing and ability to exercise control at least at the local level. So of a lesser degree there probably could be said of the Catholic church but certainly not until very late in the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but during the Austro-Hungarian empire in the institutional sense could Bosnia in any way decide its destiny?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not comfortable with the notion of Bosnia as an animated entity. You began this question by asking about the peoples of Bosnia and I think I can answer that question. There was autonomy granted under Austro-Hungarian rule to the Serbian church and school communes in, I think, 1909 and to the Muslim religious and cultural institutions also in 1909. In addition, the Catholic church had considerable ability to influence events in Bosnia under Austro-Hungarian rule, so at least to some of the population that viewed itself as Croatian had that right. I'm not arguing that Bosnia as a political entity had independence or sovereignty, but various peoples were able to achieve some limited control over their own destinies over that period, to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What you have been talking about is cultural autonomy. I am only interested in the political autonomy of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How could they decide their destiny during the period of the Austro-Hungarian empire? Through which institutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You lead me to the Parliament created in 1910, which had, to be sure, limited authority. It was elected, as I've indicated, on a limited franchise, and the power of the Parliament to make laws was circumscribed to some degree by the authorities, but that was the nature of political authority which the Bosnians were able to exercise during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, if we leave aside the Banovinas, the peoples who were living in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina today, could they in any way autonomously decide on their political destiny and regulate their mutual relationships?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That again is two questions. Bosnia did not have autonomy during royal Yugoslavia, but its people participated in the Parliamentary institutions of the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes from 1918 until the dictatorship was proclaimed in 1929 on a largely unrestricted basis, much as citizens of a State in the United States participate in federal political institutions. After 1929 the rules were tightened and the degree of that participation declined, but it nevertheless continued in Parliamentary representation and elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Anyway if we ignore for a moment the Middle Ages, is it correct to say that Bosnia-Herzegovina became a sovereign state for the first time in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. A few words about the war in Slovenia. On page 181 you mention that the Slovenians put up surprisingly successful resistance to the JNA and as a result the JNA with drew. So my question is: Did the JNA withdraw from Slovenia because of the surprising resistance of the Slovenes or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were a combination of reasons. The degree of resistance was indeed a surprise I think to the JNA command and certainly facilitated its decision they did not have much at stake in Slovenia. I will stay away and avoid a single causal answer to your answer. Certainly the surprising resistance by the Slovenes was important. At the same time the JNA command clearly arrived rather quickly at the conclusion that Slovenia was not central to its plans and furthermore that the detaching of Slovenia from the Yugoslav Federal Republic might have some advantages for the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But why, why was the war in Slovenia so small in scale and in Croatia much greater? Why was the fighting fiercer? Can you tell us something about the reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the circumstances in Slovenia were such that the JNA quickly arrived at a conclusion that its strategic interests were not at stake, I think a decision facilitated by the surprising resistance. This decision was not one that the JNA reached in Croatia or Bosnia. The reasons that it reached those conclusions in Croatia and Bosnia are again several. Certainly of vital importance was the concern for the Serbian population that existed both in Croatia and Bosnia and the then developing relationship between certain officers in the JNA command and the Serbian political movements in the Krajina and the paramilitary organisations that had been trained in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned the strategic interest of the JNA. You mentioned paramilitary Serbian organisations in Krajina. Could you explain why it was in the strategic interests of the JNA to go to war in Croatia and prevent secession and it was not in its strategic interest to prevent the secession of Slovenia, because according to its constitution the JNA should have preserved the unit of Yugoslavia. So that is the difference in the strategic interests of the JNA in Slovenia and in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what the constitution has to do with the interests of the JNA. The JNA was in the position of evaluating various positions. I really can't present to you -- present myself as an expert as to what happened within the JNA at that time and would be reluctant to make an assessment about its strategic interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but you did mention the strategic interests. Let me re-word that question. The Serbs' plan to determine the western borders of Serbia, did they in any event involve Slovenia in any sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we find the reasons for the lack of interest of the JNA in the secession of Slovenia therein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One might.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. When, according to you, did the Yugoslav people's army begin its interview in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't fix a date for it. The Yugoslav National Army was obviously posted in Bosnia from the time of World War II, and so had, you know, serious facilities, production facilities, troop facilities, large numbers of troops in Bosnia that had been there all along. It intensified their presence in Bosnia in the course of the war in Croatia, but I can't really give you specifics of that effort on the part of the JNA. I think it's difficult to state a date that a group that was there from the beginning or from some time can be said to be directly intervening. That was more of a progressive process that occurred over some time rather than a single date in which it was initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps we could mention some of the more remarkable events. Do you know when the JNA destroyed the Croatian village of Ravno, at least the year? It is a village in Bosnia-Herzegovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: October of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know when 10,000 reservists from Serbia and Montenegro were deployed on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not into the barracks but on the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was some time in the Fall of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know when the JNA arrested Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not too sure where you're going with these questions. I can answer "yes" and "no" to your interrogation of my knowledge of these events but if you're trying to ask for a series of developments, I think it would be better to speak about this progression of events as a holistic process. As I've indicated, the mobilisation of the JNA intensified in Bosnia in the Fall of 1991. That took -- there were several dimensions to that. One was the creation of the so-called Serbian military areas, which took place in September of 1991, and secured greater military control of some civilian areas and positioned the JNA to better prosecute the war in Croatia. Then this role of the JNA along the border areas of Croatia in particular became very important in the way that the war was waged in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm trying to see when the JNA started its preparations for the conflict, and I think you've answered that question. Do you know when a state of war was proclaimed by the government in Sarajevo and against whom? Who was designated the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When a state of war was proclaimed in Sarajevo, I believe it was 7th April 1991. I'm not certain. I can't give you that date with certainty -- or 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know when the first attack of the JNA was launched on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again there are multiple dates that one can use. There were clashes beginning on March 1st and actual attacks that began by Serbian paramilitary units on April 6th, and the first attacks on Sarajevo occurred immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know which is the official date for the establishment of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? When was it formally established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you estimate whether this was before or after the attack on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 184 of the transcript you claim that Milosevic had a dispute with a part of the Bosnian Serbs in March 1993. Am I correct in saying this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have I remembered what you said well? What does that mean? Did he completely break off all relationships? Did military co-operation between Serbia and the Bosnian Serbs continue? Was there any kind of intervention by the JNA? Could you explain that a little?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, that's four questions I hear, and so could you ask me one perhaps and I'll ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. You claim that Milosevic fell out with a section of the Bosnian Serbs in March 1993. What does that exactly imply for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in March of 1993 that Milosevic asked the Bosnian Serbs to sign the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. There was considerable pressure upon the Bosnian Serbs to do that. At their so-called assembly they rejected that, and I think at that point one can say that there was a split or difference of view points between Milosevic and the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After that date did Serbia give the Bosnian Serbs military assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After that date did paramilitary units from Serbia enter Bosnia and wage war on the side of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that the preponderance of evidence would say that they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After that date did the JNA in any way directly participate in any one of the battles in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just if I can clarify the question a minute, from May of 1992 going forward the JNA in its manifestations in Bosnia became the army of the Bosnian Serbs. Therefore, although I view this as yet an extension of the JNA's military force under a different name, it did become, in fact, a force under a separate command, that of General Mladic, and the question as to whether the JNA, as it was based in Serbia and Montenegro, intervened, I think there are very strong probability that additional units entered at the time of the fight for Srebrenica in March and April 1993 but I do not have the evidence to support that sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We come to Karadordevo. You mentioned Karadordevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, perhaps we will take a break now, 20 minutes, which is what we are going to do from now on so we do not overtax the interpreters. This morning you said, Mr. Nobilo, that you thought you would cross-examine the witness for about an hour. I think it has been more than an hour now. I am not trying to time you every time you ask questions, but I do think by what your colleague said we should be finished by 5.30 and allow time for my colleagues and myself to ask questions. So how do you see the rest of the afternoon? How do you see the schedule for the rest of the afternoon, because you are the one who knows the questions you still have left to ask. We don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have another three pages of this block of mine, and it's rather difficult for me to say. I may have four or five questions and some sub-questions, but I think I will be finished in less than half an hour. At least I'll do my best to speed up things as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then we will resume at 4.30, perhaps a slightly longer break, so that you can discuss things with Mr. Hayman, and then if you take half an hour, it will take us to 5 o'clock. Mr. Hayman, you yourself, about how much time do you think you are going to need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have eliminated about a third of my material in the sake of brevity and speed, but I still think, because I have a number of documents from the witness' prior publications and writings to show him, that that is going to take a period of time, just the simple process of distributing and having some site translations of very limited portions I have highlighted. I do think it's going to take a couple of hours but I think I can do it in a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: About two hours then. Do you have any comments you would like to make about this schedule, Prosecution, because that means, of course, that Mr. Donia would have to come back tomorrow morning. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have to be here one way or the other, Judge. I think it's a matter of Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Donia is available to the International Criminal Tribunal. I suppose that's what he is going to answer, although I am sure you are tired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm at your disposal, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then we will break now. We'll start again at 4.30 for an hour and then tomorrow morning again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Donia, we had stopped at Karadordevo. You mentioned Karadordevo and the speculations of the press on an agreement between Franjo Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic on a division of Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness, microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know, are you aware of any statement made by the participants in that meeting on the substance of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you have any direct information regarding the contents of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Speculation in the media, as you said, about the agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic on the division of Bosnia, do you accept it as a historian as being correct or do you have a neutral or indifferent attitude towards that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this issue of exactly what was agreed upon at Milosevo, I have become an agnostic. I do not believe that the participants have either made a statement of sufficient clarity nor a denial that is sufficiently convincing to lead me to any firm conclusion. I would note that amongst my scholarly colleagues I'm in the minority in that regard and those who have looked at the interviews with people who were close to the participants have come to the conclusion that there was some sort of definite agreement. I'm thinking principally about the article by Atilla Hore in the East European Quarterly of April 1997 called "The Croatian Project to Partition Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1990-1994" based on interviews done by various publications in Croatia with those who were either present or were close to the participants. This is one example of an independent person who has concluded that such an agreement was reached, but I myself really can't conclude anything other than that there was extensive speculation and has been ever since in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Then perhaps as a neutral observer how would you explain that after that agreement in the summer of 1991 Vukavar took place and Dubrovnik took place, the events in Vukavar and Dubrovnik. How does this match with the agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I really do not believe it necessarily conflicts with it, because the two parties, while potentially eager to carve-up Bosnia, nevertheless were pursuing a separate agenda. Each of them was pursuing a separate agenda on the issue of Croatia. It will be remembered that the Karadordevo meeting did take place early in 1991 prior to the outbreak of hostilities in Slovenia and in Croatia, so this could be seen as one of several efforts to reach an agreement prior to the outbreak of hostilities and indeed one which might have potentially prevented them. Again I emphasise I can draw no conclusion as to exactly what agreement was reached at Karadordevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 208 of the transcript you said that the Republika Srpska and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were very similar. It is lines 1-5. Briefly could you tell us what is the main reason of the formation of the Serb Republic? What is its aim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, in the statement that I made I said that the Croatian Community was engaging in an act at this time that was remarkably similar to what the Serbs were doing at the very same time, establishing a separate community on a purely territorial basis. Your basis was what was the purpose of the creation of the Srkpsa Republika and its purpose was to establish a separate territorial entity within Bosnia, which certainly in the Bosnian Serb conception was one to be dominated by the Bosnian Serbs or inhabited exclusively by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The founders of Republika Srpska, did they have a further aim of unification with The Republic of Serbia, or were they satisfied with establishing their own entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they probably had an ultimate aim of unification with Serbia, but were not in a position to pursue that agenda at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But did they officially declare that as being their objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was the main aim of the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Why it was founded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it was founded for a couple of reasons, but I would observe that it had the express purpose of establishing a territorial entity of Bosnian Croats very similar to the Serbian objectives at the time, a separate territorial entity dominated by, if not exclusively inhabited by, Bosnia's Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When establishing these facts did you have any contact with the legal documents of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the founding documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I also took note of Lord Owen's observation that in his view the objectives being pursued by the Croatian Community were not only similar to but, in fact, modelled on those of the Srkpsa Republika.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us in the founding act of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna what is stated to be the reason for the formation of that community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have that document at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me regarding the legal documents of Herceg-Bosna did that community recognise being a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. When were the three autonomous Serbian regions established? Could you tell us the dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And when was the Republika Srpska founded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have the exact date. I believe it was early 1992, perhaps January. In that range.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you accept January 9th, 1992 as the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will accept it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in your assessment whether the government in Sarajevo started in time to prepare for defence against the aggression of the JNA, the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You spoke about dual citizenship and you claimed on page 211 of the transcript, like 17-21, that dual citizenship -- I'm citing from memory -- that it was envisaged only for those living in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the report that was carried in the press at the time of the two resolutions that were passed at this meeting on 9th February, the one regarding dual citizenship on the territory of Herceg-Bosna and the second regarding the upcoming referendum for independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have you seen those documents in their original form, the documents you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've seen the press report. I forget the paper that carried it. I believe it was Vjesnik. It may have been Slobodna Dalmatia. One of those two newspapers carried a report on the resolution of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and the law on citizenship that all Croats, regardless of where they live in the world, are entitled to Croatian citizenship in addition to the citizenship of the country of their residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Pursuant to the law and the constitution, can a Croat from Sarajevo have a Croatian citizenship just like a Croat from Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're asking me a constitutional question. My impression is that under the Croatian constitution and this extraordinary provision that one could. One could have that citizenship in Australia or Micronesia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On page 215 you talk about the territorial objectives of the HDZ instead of the cultural objectives and the cultural community of Bosnian Croats. Do you think that it was appropriate in 1991 and 1992 to focus on the formation of a cultural community or rather a community that would defend the territory on which one lives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not only do I think that it was appropriate to focus on a cultural community, but I would cite interviews by the chief Franciscan in Bosnia, Petar Anjelovic, and Bishop Pujic of Sarajevo, who in March and July of 1993 both condemned in exclusionary policy of a territorial emphasis abandoning these hundreds of thousands of Croats outside the territorial unit of Herceg-Bosna. I share their view that this is inappropriate, was in 1992 and still would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in the course of 1992 and 1993 how many Bosniaks and Croats fled from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your question was how many Croats or Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Bosniaks and Croats, both ethnic groups as inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a number that's a little bit contested. The number frequently used for refugees created was 2 million. Many of those were refugees who were driven from their homes but remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but a good probably half or more of those were indeed driven from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and accepted in refugees in neighbouring countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. Your Honour, that would be all I have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree when war broke out in Bosnia in March of 1992 the JNA and/or Bosnian Serbs enjoyed an overwhelming advantage in weaponry and personnel over the combined forces of the Bosnian Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The JNA or Bosnian Serbs had about 90,000 troops in Bosnia at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's a good number to -- it's a good estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the JNA also controlled most armies and munition stock piles and could rely on over 40 planes and hundreds of tanks. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: By contrast the Bosnian Croat militia had about how many men under arms in that time period, if any, March/April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Croat militia, I'm not certain -- I wouldn't be certain of that number without consulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of your book with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Bosnia and Herzegovina,: a tradition betrayed"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you to see if the passage at page 239 refreshes your recollection with respect to the number of men under arms in the Bosnian Croat militia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I cite the figure 12,000 in western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now west Herzegovina, that's a good distance from Central Bosnia; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's more than 10 or 20 or even 50 kms from Central Bosnia to western Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many men under arms the Bosnian Croat militia had in Central Bosnia in the time period April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had superior manpower to the Bosnian Croat militia. Would you agree with that proposition as of April 1992, superior in numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The territorial forces certainly had more nominal participants than in the Croatian militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And there were about 50,000 of those. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of varying degrees of preparation, participation and weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now when you say territorial forces, are you referring to the indigenous reserve, if you will, forces that existed throughout Yugoslavia prior to the war in 1992, the wars in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
