utterances.text: Do you know was the -- if you know, was the Bosnian Croat militia in Central Bosnia also born from the territorial forces, just like the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was born from the territorial forces in that region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You do not know the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe otherwise that the Bosnian Croat militia in Central Bosnia was not born from the territorial forces that existed in that region?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. I mean, the witness just said he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, would you reformulate your question or do you want to ask the question as you asked it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, I asked did he have any reason to doubt that the Bosnian Croat militia was from the territorial forces. I will rephrase it, your Honour. Do you have any information to the contrary, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just know very little about the actual formation of the HVO in Bosnia. I just can't answer the question. I have no reason to believe otherwise but have no reason to believe that was the case either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were the members of the territorial force or forces, were they professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were in a sense trained reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they reservists, if you know, that had a regular period of duty, such as one month a year or 20 weekends a year, or was that not part of the territorial force structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were not full-time forces. I do not know what their annual obligations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether all men between certain ages were actually members of the territorial force in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that was the original intent in theory but to the extent to which it became reality I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the members of the territorial forces had firearms issued to them? In other words did they have their own firearm in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they possessed any modern communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the concept of the territorial forces was that they would defend their own local area in case of an attack by an aggressor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was certainly the theory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree that's inconsistent with the concept of a mobile fighting force that will move outside of its local area in order to fight an aggressor on another terrain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think it is inconsistent. It's certainly not part of a unified theory. The territorial forces were in the event of an invasion were clearly not expected to remain within 1 km or 2 of their homes, but neither were they a highly mobile force designed to move all the way across the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You referred in your direct testimony to the process by which greater combat capability was achieved by the territorial forces as a process that occurred over approximately three years. If you would like to look at that testimony, that's on page 187, line 18: do you see that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you know, was that greater strength or combat capability gained over a three year period because soldiers acquired more training over those three years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was a number of factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would that have been one of the factors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They acquired certainly more training; they acquired more weapons; they acquired certain mobile capabilities that they didn't have before. So that process did, in fact, move forward within Bosnia for those forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would their potency, if you will, also have changed and improved as they learned matters such as discipline, military discipline, what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the end of this three year time period that you have outlined, which would have been roughly in 1995, would the army or armies that grew out of the territorial forces, would they have been comparable, in your opinion, to mature armies in western Europe, the British army or other armies, the America army, something like that, or would there still have been a gap in terms of the maturity and level of professionalism between those two groups of fighting forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've addressed in my direct testimony two issues, the Croatian army and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I would just like to note that there was some difference between the two in that Croatian forces had much greater access to modern weaponry and the Croatian army under the very strong campaign to regain its strength probably developed greater capabilities than the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in this period that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm asking you, though, about the elements that grew out of the territorial forces. You've said that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina grew out of the territorial forces of the former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you've said you do not know whether the HVO in Central Bosnia also grew out of the territorial forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So focusing for the moment on that force or forces that grew out of the territorial forces that existed in the former Yugoslavia, would you say that as of the end of this three year period you have outlined in roughly 1995, would the force or forces that resulted from this process of elevation have been comparable to a modern army in western Europe, or would there still have been a gap between those two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in no way comparable to a west European army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that because there would still have been a gap in terms of the level of training of those two groups of soldiers? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among other factors, yes. Training, weaponry, ammunition. So a variety of factors inhibited the growth of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the overall level of professionalism and discipline would also have been different from that in a modern western European army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very different kind of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with the proposition that roads in Central Bosnia have historically been of critical military significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In fact, they were very important to the German occupiers, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were important to the Austrian forces who invaded and occupied back in 1878, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And similarly, were they very important -- that is they were of strategic military significance -- in the conflict that erupted in Central Bosnia between Croats and Muslims? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that that conclusion would apply, for example, to the road from Busovaca to Travnik in Central Bosnia? Would you consider that to be an important artery between two cities of some size?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that there were roughly 1 million refugees within Bosnia that remained within Bosnia at some point in time. I didn't catch the time. Roughly when would that have been? By what point would there have been 1 million refugees? If you wish to discuss your recollection, you do discuss this issue at the top of page 245 in your book. I recognise it's late in the day, Mr. Donia, and I'm not going to make your examination a memory quiz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just appreciate your reading the book. The flow of refugees rapidly increased after April of 1992 and I have indicated that by the Fall of 1992 that about 2 million refugees had been created.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree with the proposition that about 1 million of those remained in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one time or another, yes. Again that was a progressive process that many of them fled or left and so taking a snapshot in time is probably difficult. It was a process, but I think my point in making the statement in the book was that Bosnia itself carried a very heavy refugee burden, along with the countries to which many of these refugees fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And it was an extraordinarily heavy burden, was it not, the burden from these refugees, the burden, for example, on municipal services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Providing the minimum wherewithal to these individuals placed a huge burden on the authorities in the areas in which these refugees came; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now do you know with any specificity whether, in fact, central Bosnia was the recipient, if you will, of a substantial inflow of refugees during the latter part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, let us think about that for a movement. Eastern Bosnia was in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs by the Fall of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Northern Bosnia -- let me take exception to all of Eastern Bosnia. There were still numerous enclaves which had large populations of Muslims who were subsequently to become refugees. Some of them were already refugees from villages then controlled by the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's step back one step. When war broke out, would you agree that within a matter of weeks the Bosnian Serbs occupied, took over approximately 65 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And did they necessarily create a vast movement of refugees by virtue of that action which they took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did their actions during that early period in the war include actions in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And in northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and in the western --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And in north-west Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And would you agree that simple geometry would suggest that refugees fleeing these movements would in part at least tend to flow in towards Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's speculation. I do not really know enough about the flow of refugees in that part of the country to answer your question. My experience in looking at some other areas was that refugees tended to flow along the areas of easiest egress and into towns with which they were familiar, for example from Eastern Bosnia there was a great flow into Tuzla, which was the city most familiar to refugees in that part of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me change the subject. We have a little bit of time remaining and I'll try and use it efficiently, if I may. You testified during your direct examination concerning a so-called ultimatum, which you characterised as an ultimatum which gave a deadline of April 15th, 1993. Do you recall that testimony generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you read in your testimony portions of a news article, one or more news articles, which I believe were Exhibits 25 and 26. I do not know that you'll need to refer to them, but perhaps they could be placed in front of the witness for ease of reference, if necessary. Do you have a summary of the agreement, so we can continue while those are being put in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very good. There are how many points according to this news story in this "ultimatum"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The draft agreement contains six points. I would point out that the two documents, one an article from Slobodna Dalmatia and the other an article from Vjesnik apparently share more in common than those six points. That is there is a declaration of sorts that was issued by the Croatian Defence Council and which is reflected in both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So there are six points; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: According to the news stories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Point one in essence, would you agree it is that all misunderstandings between the Croat and Muslim nation that is in Bosnia concerning borders, etc., have been resolved? Is that the first point in essence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The language is that all misunderstandings have been avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So there are no further misunderstandings. That's the essence of point one; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now point two, would you agree that the essence is that external forces, that is forces that did not originate from within a particular area, must leave that area within three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now I want to clarify the nature of this document that we're looking at. It is a quoted six point draft agreement, which has been signed by one party and not the other. Your statement of the nature of the first and second points I accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Fine. Would you agree that that second point would mean that if, for example, there was a garrison of troops that was permanently posted, for example, in the town of Zenica and had been raised from persons in that area, that garrison of troops would not have to leave that area under point two of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now point three, would you agree, provides that in each of the provinces under the Vance-Owen plan, of the six provinces that were designated as so-called Croat or Muslim provinces, that in each one command would be exercised by either the HVO or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina over all HVO and army of Bosnia and Herzegovina forces within that province or canton? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that a unitary command structure of this type would be more effective, would have been more effective in co-ordinating the common defence against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now point four, would you agree that in essence that point obliges the headquarters of the HVO and that of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to form a joint headquarters by April 15th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it does not oblige the staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to do so because it was not signed by Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It would under the terms of the agreement; accepting it for the moment as under the four corners of the agreement, that's what's proposed or contemplated by point four; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then point 5 is in essence a point that states: "There shall be no further conflict"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Point 6 provides for free passage of people and goods; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After this proposal was out in the media after about April 3rd, 1993, did President Izetbegovic speak out and reject this proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to point out that these six points do not stand in isolation in this document. This document was not circulated in the media by itself. It was circulated as part of a broader declaration by the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which involved specific steps regarding its implementation. Thus, as far as what President Izetbegovic knew about it or was given the opportunity to sign, that is not clear from this document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you do not believe that this agreement in terms, the six points we have just described, that that ever existed as a separate document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you ever seen it before, the agreement with the six points we have discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I've only seen the press reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could the usher assist in placing an exhibit before the witness, your Honour? There's also a French translation, so perhaps these two exhibits could be marked in a co-ordinated manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Usher, would you make sure that the exhibits are numbered correctly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. This is D/6 and D/6A is the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have occasion, Mr. Donia, before testifying to meet and confer with the representatives of the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the course of those conferences did you discuss the issue of this so-called ultimatum that you have subscribed to in these two news reports, Exhibits 25 and 26? Was that subject discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At any time did representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor tell you that they had in their possession this joint statement, which is exhibit D6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This statement in this form?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In this form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They didn't show it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And they didn't tell you that they had it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When did you first conclude that this so-called ultimatum and the "deadline" of April 15th, 1993 was of great significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first concluded that there was a deadline of great significance when I went to the Foreign Broadcast Information Service Reports for the period from late March to mid-April 1993 and at that time I noted a report which indicated that there was an ultimatum in effect, and that further led me to want to confirm its existence in the periodic press of the time and then, in fact, to request the Prosecution research team anything that would confirm the existence of that ultimatum and this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I take it the Prosecution gave you Exhibits 25 and 26; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You did not turn those up as a result of your own research and study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did turn up the ultimatum itself as a result of my own research and study. I specifically -- I asked the Prosecution team, in particular Milan Andrejevic, who is very familiar with those press -- the periodical press in that time to confirm the existence of that ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you find Exhibits 25 and 26 or did the Prosecution provide them to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Prosecution provided them to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say you found an "ultimatum", are you stating that you found reported in press reports of an "ultimatum"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is there any mention in your book of this so-called ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your book is over 300 pages in length. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that's true despite the fact you state in the preface or introduction that: "Our account is intended to shed light on the sources of the Bosnian conflict that began in early 1992". Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was indeed the intent of the book. It is unfortunately not a comprehensive account and there are many, many omissions in that volume. I could tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In fact, in your book do you attribute the conflict that broke out in April of 1993 between Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims to other factors than this so-called ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I mention a number of factors in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And this so-called ultimatum is not one of them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I was unaware of that ultimatum at the time I penned those lines in the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Has your opinion and views changed and now you do believe this so-called ultimatum was a critical factor in sparking conflict between Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Other than the Prosecution investigators and other representatives of the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor, have you interviewed a single participant in either the political arena or the military arena in Central Bosnia on this issue of whether this agreement was viewed as an ultimatum or not, and whether it had any role in sparking conflict between Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats? Have you interviewed a single participant in those events on that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In your meetings with the Office of the Prosecutor did they tell you that they had represented to the confirming Judge in this case that, in fact, this agreement, which is exhibit D/6, was reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Would you ask that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you that they represented to the confirming Judge, that is the Judge who confirms the indictment in this matter, that this agreement was reached and entered into by President Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not so represent to me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could the usher assist in distributing additional exhibits, your Honour? Again there's an English and a French version. (Handed). Could the Registrar provide the exhibit numbers, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D/7 and D/7A.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Donia, these are materials from which non-pertinent portions have been redacted. What remains, have you had a chance to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before, exhibit D/7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you ever discussed it with anyone from the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor, the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You stated in your direct testimony that you believed this six point agreement would be wholly unacceptable, or words to that effect, on the part of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to see my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How would you put it? You voiced some sentiment in that direction. You can pick your own words. How would you put it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never been certain about the original drafting of this document and the specific time of authorship and persons of authorship are not and haven't been at any point known to me. So I have looked at it and believed it was very much in the kind of spirit of what was going on as the HVO pushed forward for a resolution of the jurisdictional issues at that time. It certainly was not something that Alija Izetbegovic and the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina would eagerly put forward. At the same time it was in the -- particularly point four, which pertains to a joint headquarters, it was very much in accord with the announcement of President Izetbegovic in Zagreb a few days before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Speaking out in favour of a joint headquarters, so that a more co-ordinated and effective resistance to the Serbian aggression could be mounted by the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you put words in his mouth. I think he emerged from the meeting with President Tudjman and Mr. Boban having the announcement that this had been agreed upon, and certainly the pressures on him at that point were a factor in his reaching that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you are unsure whether the six points in this agreement would or would not have been unacceptable to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that with regards to point four, I have no doubt that it was acceptable and desirable. With regards to the other points, I think that the enthusiasm -- there would be certainly rapid agreement on point one, much less agreement on point two, much less eagerness on the part of the government to endorse point two, and the same point with point three and certainly strong agreement on point four -- excuse me -- five and six.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have reached 5.30. If this is a convenient breaking point ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Oui. I thought we would be able to break at this point. We will resume tomorrow at 10 o'clock with the continued cross-examination of Mr. Donia. The court stands adjourned until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: --ooOoo--
